subsubtopic: NORTHWEST TELEPHONE-CALL TO MEET REQUIREMENTS OF LICENCE-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, a company called Northwest Telephone operates as a subsidiary of CN Telecommunications. It is supplying telephone service for a large area of northeastern British Columbia adjacent to the Alaska highway. The company is charging individual Canadians a $680 fee for a simple hook-up and is not in a position even to provide such service. 1 therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Patterson):
That for reasons of total neglect and failure to provide even the most basic service dictated by the licence under which Northwest Telephone operates in northeastern British Columbia, the company be given six months from this day to implement a service which not only fulfils the requirement of the licence but is consistent with the company's widely advertised policy whereby their service to the public is not only a business but a responsibility; and that failing the company's compliance with this requirement, the licence will be revoked.

EFFECT OF INCREASED TAXES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 rise to propose a motion of urgent importance under the provisions of Standing Order 43. On this Hallowe'en day and in view of this government's trick or treat budget which brings many tricks and no treats to all the people of Canada, 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Miss Carney):
That the government be directed to stop deceiving Canadians with charlatan trickery and to admit that the proposed natural gas tax is not only a tax on natural gas exports but is also a direct and discriminatory tax on every natural gas consumer in the four western provinces and Ontario; and to admit also that

October 31, 1980
this tax will increase the domestic heating costs of western Canadians by at least 16 per cent effective tomorrow, with the increase doubling to 33 per cent or more than $150 per home by next winter; and finally, to admit to the government's shame that there will be no program of compensation to the thousands of low-income Canadians who will be faced with these sharply increased energy costs.

The recently released report of the Canada Council emphasises that in constant dollar terms the resources available to the arts through the Canada Council in 1979-80 were about the same as they were in 1975. Because of inflation and increasing operating costs, even our best publishing houses, theatres, orchestras and other basic arts institutions are in danger. That during these times of culture building in Canada, this House instructs the Secretary of State to ensure that adequate funding is received by those individuals and organizations who have achieved stature in the arts community, and especially by new companies, younger artists and those working on the frontiers of arts and communications.

subtopic: STATEMENT OF PREMIER LOUGHEED ON NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM-GOVERNMENT POSITION

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: STATEMENT OF PREMIER LOUGHEED ON NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. Last night, in responding to the budget of the Minister of Finance, the Premier of Alberta indicated that Alberta will cut its oil production by 15 per cent, will challenge the federal tax on natural gas in the courts and put on hold the Alsands project, which is necessary if Canada is to achieve energy self-sufficiency, which all of us on all sides of the House seek.
Will the federal government, in the interests of all Canadians, take advantage of the three-month period before the first cutback and renew discussions with the province of Alberta?
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: STATEMENT OF PREMIER LOUGHEED ON NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on the gas throughput tax we understand that Premier Lougheed does want to take the matter up in the courts. We think that is a very reasonable and rational approach, and we are anxious to see any differences as to the law on the constitution interpreted by the courts.
In so far as the tar sands are concerned, we are a bit disappointed because the budget did indicate a $38 per barrel price, which is about the world price now. It seemed to be reasonably acceptable on all sides. It did indicate that production could be financially viable, and we are disappointed that Premier Lougheed seems to have some reservations about that. But he did not indicate any precise response so, of course, we will have to wait to see what he has in mind, and we are anxious to discuss the matter further with him.
In so far as the cutbacks are concerned, as the hon. member says, they would not be effective until they begin three months from now, and we welcome this breathing space, perhaps to continue negotiations with the province of Alberta. We will see if any accommodation is possible. 1 hope it is and we will certainly bend every effort in that direction.

subtopic: STATEMENT OF PREMIER LOUGHEED ON NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: STATEMENT OF PREMIER LOUGHEED ON NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I gather that the Prime Minister is moving in the direction of some discussion and conciliation. If he is saying that that is in the best interests of Canada, I just want him to know that we share that view.

subtopic: STATEMENT OF PREMIER LOUGHEED ON NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: STATEMENT OF PREMIER LOUGHEED ON NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Can the Prime Minister indicate to the House if it is possible to say today or tomorrow, given the short period of time, when those discussions might begin and whether he will involve himself in these matters?
In order that the jurisdiction can be tested with respect to the gas tax, which 1 agree is a matter of law pure and simple, could the Prime Minister indicate whether he, in the course of early discussions, would use his offices or whatever his legal powers are to bring those matters to court quickly so that they can be settled?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: STATEMENT OF PREMIER LOUGHEED ON NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Yes, Madam Speaker, as far as we are able we would be anxious to have the legal aspect of this matter decided as expeditiously as possible. 1 will be discussing with the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Minister of Justice the ways in which this can be done. It presumably will involve an early contact with Alberta to establish on what it wants to base its case and how it thinks it would want to proceed.
With regard to the tar sands, I hope that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources will be able to contact his opposite number reasonably soon because we are not clear what Alberta has in mind when it talks about increased royalties and so forth. If it is a regime which, in effect, prevents the private sector from exploiting the tar sands, we would think it a regrettable move because, as we know, all of

October 31, 1980
Oral Questions
Canada is relying on the tar sands and the heavy oils to reach self-sufficiency by the end of the decade.
On the third point, I am afraid I cannot indicate any particular response at this time. On the matter of the interruption of oil supplies, many questions arise. The first is whether it is constitutional. Is it within the power of a province to interrupt the free flow of commodities across the country? I will want to study that at some length with the Minister of Justice and perhaps in cabinet before indicating any response.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: STATEMENT OF PREMIER LOUGHEED ON NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, with regard to the last matter discussed by the Prime Minister I think there are very few Canadians who would view the courtroom as the appropriate place to settle a difference within the family, and I am talking about the Canadian family. I am talking about the last matter. 1 hope the Prime Minister might take an initiative in this matter with respect to those discussions.
Having regard to the history of matters, I hope the Prime Minister will consider that with respect to the tar sands it is a matter he himself might raise in initiating any discussions. The purpose of my question is to ask the Prime Minister, in the best interests of the country, to take the initiative in these discussions and to take it rather quickly.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: STATEMENT OF PREMIER LOUGHEED ON NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Well, Madam Speaker, I do not think I can add anything to the previous answer. I fail to see how the hon. member can argue that, in one case, Premier Lougheed is right in taking us to court, but in the other case we would not be right in taking him to court because it suddenly becomes a family matter.

subtopic: STATEMENT OF PREMIER LOUGHEED ON NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: STATEMENT OF PREMIER LOUGHEED ON NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: I apologize if I misunderstood the hon. member. Perhaps he could repeat the question and the preface.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: STATEMENT OF PREMIER LOUGHEED ON NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Just so it is absolutely clear, Madam Speaker, let me point out that there may be some areas where the courtroom would be the appropriate place. The thrust of my question is that in most areas the courtroom is not the appropriate place if one has a substitute, and that substitute, in my judgment and in my respectful submission, Madam Speaker, is the bargaining table. I am asking the Prime Minister whether he would assure the House that he will take steps immediately to take the initiative to go back to the bargaining table so that a settlement can be produced in the Canadian family with respect to a matter which must be vexing to every Canadian.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: STATEMENT OF PREMIER LOUGHEED ON NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Well, I did understand the hon. member correctly, Madam Speaker, and he did suggest that, in the case of the gas tax, the court is the proper route, but that in the case of the curtailment of production, the court was not the proper route. I am suggesting that we are examining all routes and I do not exclude either an appeal to the courts by Alberta or an appeal to the courts by us.
However, I do repeat what I said at the outset, that further negotiations are certainly appropriate and they will be embarked upon as soon as cabinet has had a chance to examine the real substance of Premier Lougheed's answer. Some of it can be ascertained by initial discussions; some may have to be ascertained in other ways.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM-INQUIRY RESPECTING FEDERAL INITIATIVES WITH ALBERTA
NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM-INQUIRY RESPECTING FEDERAL INITIATIVES WITH ALBERTA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to pursue the line of questioning of the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton and I wish to direct my question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. It relates to the questions I was putting to him yesterday on the matter of security of supply.
In his document "The National Energy Program", the importance of non-conventional oils in the program is very clear. It will result in a greater degree of production than the conventional sources of supply, and that to me is the key area of concern and one on which we should be focussing our attention.
My question to the minister is, what initiatives is he proposing to take in the context of a broad energy negotiation with the province of Alberta which will result in those important projects in western Canada being brought forward, projects which will help security of supply in eastern and central Canada as well as create jobs, not just in the narrow context of the non-conventional projects but in the broad context of a total agreement?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM-INQUIRY RESPECTING FEDERAL INITIATIVES WITH ALBERTA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member is quite right that the non-conventional oil is our main source of growth of supply in the coming decade. Those projects have a long lead time. The next tar sands plant could not come into operation before 1987. This does not mean that we shall not attach a very high priority to those projects. In the last two weeks I have had meetings with representatives of both the Cold Lake project and the oil sands project and I am supposed to have further discussions with them before very long. Also, my officials are in contact with them.
As the Prime Minister has just indicated, as contained in our budget and as I indicated at the last meeting I had with the minister of energy of Alberta, we put forward an offer which we felt was not only fair but also high enough to ensure that the projects would be economically viable. There have been further representations from the industry. We are still in the course of discussions, but obviously these are major investments and, quite clearly, there is need for further discussions, not only with the industry but also with the government of Alberta, particularly in light of Premier Lougheed's statement last night about his plans for the oilsands.

subtopic: NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM-INQUIRY RESPECTING FEDERAL INITIATIVES WITH ALBERTA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the minister. In the proposal which the province of Alberta put forward toward the end of July, I believe they
October 31, 1980

allowed for a $7 billion investment in the next three oil sands projects, both in the debt and equity as well as the total commencement of the infrastructure. Since the province of Alberta is such a critical partner in bringing forward these projects, is it possible for the minister to broaden the sweep of these negotiations to include not just those projects themselves, but in the total concept of the energy policy to bring the province back as a willing partner in the very important developments we must have in the country?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM-INQUIRY RESPECTING FEDERAL INITIATIVES WITH ALBERTA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, certainly I would have no objection to that. As a matter of fact, we have talked about those two projects because they are the ones currently on the table on which tens of millions of dollars have already been spent. But as the hon. member knows, Nova and Petro-Canada have a joint proposal for a fourth plant. Certainly we would be very interested in discussing further proposals, if there are any, with the government of Alberta, or industry, or both.
As for possible investment by the government of Alberta, obviously this is a matter for the government of Alberta to decide. At the present time, on those projects the problem does not appear to be essentially a shortage of money for investment; it is the assurance that there will be a good enough rate of return on whatever they will invest, and that is what is still being discussed.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER PRIME MINISTER WILL MEET PREMIER LOUGHEED
INQUIRY WHETHER PRIME MINISTER WILL MEET PREMIER LOUGHEED
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Many Canadians find it unacceptable that we have a confrontation and deterioration in federal-provincial relations. I think last night was just a further stage in this process. I detect in the House today a feeling that what is needed is a calm and reasoned approach by both the federal government and Alberta because the people of Canada are caught in the middle of this dispute.
The Prime Minister appeared to indicate that he would keep the door open to negotiations, and then there was some talk from the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources about officials meeting. Would he clarify for the House and for the country what specific plans he has in mind for further negotiations? More specifically, is he prepared to meet with Premier Lougheed personally, and when?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER PRIME MINISTER WILL MEET PREMIER LOUGHEED
speechtext: Madam Speaker, it seems to me that that question is something of a repetition of the question asked by the opposition House leader.

subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER PRIME MINISTER WILL MEET PREMIER LOUGHEED
speechtext: No, not quite.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER PRIME MINISTER WILL MEET PREMIER LOUGHEED
speechtext:
He has my answers. They might be more enlightened if I knew the position of the hon. member on this. He seems puzzled by the whole situation, as indeed he should be. The take of the producing provinces is reduced from something like 45 per cent to 43 per cent, which is not major.
Oral Questions
The take of the federal government is considerably increased, but it is at the expense of the producing private sector. It would be interesting to know if the NDP will support our approach on this, if it thinks we are hitting the private sector and the oil companies too hard, if it thinks as a consequence that the federal government should be getting less money from them, or if it thinks we should be hitting them harder. I await some help from the hon. member who has a distinguished record of thought on this matter.

subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER PRIME MINISTER WILL MEET PREMIER LOUGHEED
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER PRIME MINISTER WILL MEET PREMIER LOUGHEED
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I might say to the Prime Minister that we on this side of the House feel the provinces have legitimate concerns for their vast problems and costs. If one has been to Fort McMurray, as has the Prime Minister, one will know the cost of schools, housing, social services and so on. At the same time we recognize, as do most Canadians, that we must have a national energy policy.
The Prime Minister answered my question with a question, which I know is a favourite technique. But the point which 1 think the country wants to know is: will he personally continue negotiations with Premier Lougheed? Will he personally meet with Premier Lougheed and, if so, when?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER PRIME MINISTER WILL MEET PREMIER LOUGHEED
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I met with Premier Lougheed for a few days last summer and I was prepared to meet with him last Monday. I am prepared to meet with him again.

subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER PRIME MINISTER WILL MEET PREMIER LOUGHEED
speechtext: When?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER PRIME MINISTER WILL MEET PREMIER LOUGHEED
speechtext: Any time which would be useful from his point of view and mine. He can come tomorrow if he wishes. The point is that the hon. member seems to be making suggestions which do not have any substance to them. The real question is: is the sharing fair or not? If the provincial share is going down from 45 to 43 per cent, it is not a big stroke against the provinces, or against the schools in Fort McMurray, which seem to concern the hon. member. But there is a rather big take from the oil companies which is to the benefit of the consumers of Canada.

subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER PRIME MINISTER WILL MEET PREMIER LOUGHEED
speechtext: Oh, come on!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER PRIME MINISTER WILL MEET PREMIER LOUGHEED
speechtext: And to the federal government. I am prepared to meet Premier Lougheed. It would be of help to me if the hon. member himself-I know his party is divided on this- could tell me if he thinks we are taking too much from the oil companies or too much from the province when we are going down to 43 per cent. I am not asking a question; I am just suggesting that he might try to get his thoughts together and be helpful to the Canadian nation on this.

subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER PRIME MINISTER WILL MEET PREMIER LOUGHEED
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister mentioned Canadian consumers, who appear to me to be the forgotten people in this dispute, if I can put my thoughts together.

Oral Questions
1 have a question for the Prime Minister. Canadian consumers are being hit by a $340 increase per family for energy costs, for the cost of heating their homes and being able to drive their cars next year as a result of the Prime Minister's budget. Would the Prime Minister consider introducing a cost of living tax credit to help these middle and low-income Canadian consumers?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER PRIME MINISTER WILL MEET PREMIER LOUGHEED
speechtext: The hon. member thinks the consumer is being asked to pay prices which are too high. Is he then siding with the federal government against the producing provinces and saying that, as Premier Lougheed is asking for even higher prices, 1 should meet him, as the hon. member suggests, and turn down his requests for higher prices? This is the kind of guidance I am asking for from the hon. member.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. The Minister has often said in the past that users of heating oil must be encouraged to convert to gas. subtopic: INCENTIVES TO QUEBECKERS TO ABANDON OIL HEATING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the national energy program clearly states that the government would subsidize, up to $800, home owners who would convert their existing oil heating system to an alternate source of energy. Those other forms of energy are especially natural gas and electricity.
We are quite willing to subsidize those two forms of energy and make them accessible to all. But we must do it in co-operation with the provincial authorities, and the provincial authority concerned must accept that its hydro company, Hydro-Quebec in this instance, make the conversions involved. That does not depend on us; each provincial government is responsible for deciding whether or not it is willing to encourage the use of its hydroelectricity to heat homes.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I shall be very brief. My question of privilege arises from question period last Tuesday, October 21, when I put questions to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc), the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro), and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
I shall quote briefly from pages 3870 and 3871 of Hansard. The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans indicated that he had received the report that I was questioning him about and that he would "-have a fuller answer for the hon. member early next week." In my view, Madam Speaker, that would be Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development said, within the text, that he was seriously considering a public inquiry and that "-discussions will be going on before I will be required to make any decision of that kind."
The Right Hon. Prime Minister said "-we asked for a review-".
I will give a very brief preamble, Madam Speaker, to the concerns that I have in my question of privilege. In 1977 the effluent mining liquid regulations were passed by this House. In mid-election last year, when Parliament was not sitting, regulations which strayed dramatically from legislation passed
October 31, 1980

by this House, were made by order in council. These regulations are disputed by independent scientists, lawyers, fishermen, native people, the Anglican and Catholic Churches of Canada, environmental groups, the public, and members of this House. The passage of this special order in council infringes on the rights and privileges of myself and, in my view, of all members of this House.
Yesterday I gave the minister 24 hours' notice of this question of privilege, precisely where it was in Hansard, and the nature of it.
I believe that you should rule on two specific things, Madam Speaker, the first being in relation to orders that are passed when this House is not in session that give extraordinary rights or unique rights, as in this case, to major industrial developments. Part and parcel of that is whether the privileges of this House have been tampered with by the special order in council.
The second part of my question of privilege, and 1 believe the minister is prepared to respond to it today, is whether the statements made on October 21 in this House by the Prime Minister, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, are misleading to this House. The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans indicated that a statement would be forthcoming regarding a full public inquiry into the dumping of toxic tailings into Alice Arm, British Columbia. In my view that statement should be made in this House, Madam Speaker.

speakeroldname: Hon. Romeo LeBlanc (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subsubtopic: MR. FULTON-ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-MINISTERS' STATEMENTS DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I tried to take notes as the hon. member was speaking, so I hope that I did not mix up the dates he used.
I remember when the hon. member asked me about a report but I think I misunderstood. He was referring to the McCart report; I was referring to the report of my officials, of whom I had asked a review of the recommendations that had come forward in April, 1979.
Be that as it may, Madam Speaker, the officials in the Pacific region did make a review as I requested. They have now made it clear that nothing has emerged from their reexamination to lead them to change the recommendations they had made and which were eventually put into the order in council which was passed. The recommendations were that the tailings would be more safely stored at a very deep part of the Alice Arm bay and, in fact, in their judgment this was a safer approach than locating the tailings in a land-locked or land-based site where there would be very considerable bleaching.
I discussed the report with my officials at the beginning of this week when I was in British Columbia. The conclusion is the same as that arrived at some year and a half ago.
The new information is that I have written to the company stating exactly what monitoring devices would be required and what monitoring plan would be required before final approval was given.
In one of his questions the hon. member referred to the McCart report. A preliminary examination of that report
Privilege-Mr. Rose
seems to indicate that no substantive new information is provided. I am of the view, however, that the only way that the fears which exist can be contained or alleviated is by clear participation in the monitoring process. I have started discussions with my colleague, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, to see how we can involve the Nishga tribe, which is worried about this issue, in a monitoring operation, and also how we can make information fully available. That has always been my approach.
In this case, my review of the situation leads me to think that this was a matter of what was, on balance, the best judgment. Until I have been given further information I think that would still be my position.
Obviously, Madam Speaker, I would like to see the situation where there is participation and full knowledge of the monitoring operation that would be required to make sure how these tailings are being disposed of and how the situation evolved. I hope I have answered some of the hon. member's worries.

speechtext:
That this House condemns the government for having failed to harness the energies and talents of Canada's scientific and technological community in the development of an industrial strategy which would draw on Canada's traditional resource base, on our manufacturing strength, and on our new high technology industries.
He said: Madam Speaker, when preparing this motion our caucus stood back and had an over-all look at the ups and downs of the Canadian economy over the last decade or so, and the dismal inability of the budget which was presented earlier this week to come to terms effectively with the problems with which the people of this country have been trying to wrestle and find solutions. Surely we do have one of the best endowed countries in terms of resources and wealth in the world today. Surely we have a country which, compared with most other countries in the world, is one of the least developed.
We have a very young population. Our development is only 100 or less years, and we have a very thin population. There is still very, very much to be done. Yet what we have found in the last decade or so is an unemployment level which is unacceptable. It is even higher than those in more developed countries with larger populations and fewer resources. 1 think of the Scandinavian countries, Great Britain, Holland, Germany, etc. We must wonder how it is possible that a country with so much going for it can find itself in such a crippled, weak, and second-class position. Obviously the government seated opposite, which is the party which has dominated this country for the last two decades, must surely accept the major responsibility for the fact that the strength of this country has

been drained and has not been utilized, co-ordinated, or brought together to bring solutions to the problems we face.
One of the important areas of the failure of this government is that of research and development, and the failure to utilize the technological know-how of our trained university graduates. In fact, over the last decade or so we have seen continuous erosion as young people, not being able to find employment in this country, leave it and go mainly to the United States. That represents a loss of our public investment in their education. If we are going to stop the erosion of Canada's manufacturing base and improve our competitive position in the international high technological market, it is essential that we have a coherent policy on research and development.
The benefits of research and development have been well documented. They include increased employment, greater output of growth in that particular sector of the economy, improved market penetration, and lower costs to the consumer for goods with high research and development components. In a study of the performance of Canadian manufacturing industries between 1961 and 1974 the Ministry of State for Science and Technology found that research and development intensive industries had almost triple the growth rate, twice the productivity, significantly greater rates of employment and less inflation in prices than industries not engaged in research and development. It has been shown as well that for every dollar spent on research and development a return of at least $30 is produced.
Yet despite the fact that even government studies have shown the effectiveness and importance of research and development, the record of this government in that area is dismal. It is cynical. If I were a little more paranoid and thought in terms of international espionage, I would come to the conclusion that this government has deliberately sabotaged research and development in this country and weakened this country's position. How cynical this government is!
In 1968 the federal cabinet set a goal for expenditure on research and development of 2 per cent of the gross national product. The Lamontagne Senate committee in 1972 recommended that 2.5 per cent of the gross national product go to research and development by 1978. In actual fact, in that decade research and development in this country fell by some 36 per cent. Again we find that in June of 1978, the then minister in charge, Judd Buchanan, set a goal of 1.5 per cent by 1983, and this year, lo and behold, in the Speech from the Throne we have another great Liberal promise that by 1985 we will achieve the goal of 1.5 per cent. Consistently the government has paid lip service, and that is about it. That is in fact what the Liberals are known for, their lips. It is all promises and no action. The present budget is a great example of this.
What is it in the present budget that was presented to us which would bring us one step closer to the stated goal? There are no plans in place, there is no strategy outlined. It is a continuation of the same policies that this government has
followed for years and years-that is, the policy of 'do nothing', to allow the resources of this country to be shipped out, to allow the continuation of high industry and high technology being imported into this country, and to allow the continued weakening of this country, deepening our inability to make it on our own.

speechtext: And they call themselves Canadians.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE IN INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
All we have is the trappings. Yes, we have a flag, and yes, we are going to have the constitution, but the guts of the country have been sold, shipped out and drained off. We do not have the ability to determine our own economic destiny. We do not have the ability to train and employ our young people in the field of technology. All we have is lip service.
The major problem in our country today, in terms of achieving the goal of 1.5 per cent of the gross national product for research and development-which I think is even too low- is our industrial make-up. The fact is that most of the important industries in this country are nothing but branch plants, that most of the important industry in this country, such as the manufacturing industry, is controlled from outside this country. The multinationals in this country have a dismal record of research and development. It is not necessarily the fact that we have not had sufficient public funds going into this area that has caused the problem. In fact on that score we do relatively the same as other countries. But the fact is that the private sector has not been able to pull its weight in terms of research and development.
It is not the Canadian owned public sector, it is the multinational sector of the private industry that has not pulled its weight. This was admitted this year in June by the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Roberts) when he spoke to the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and said that if we are to meet our medium-term objective in research and development it will have to be through the efforts of foreign-controlled companies in this country. He went on to suggest that it will require a $2.4 billion increase in outlays on research and development, most of which will have to come from the foreign private sector. Foreign ownership is highest in Canada's research intensive industries, and it is these industries that have the highest profits. In other words, the industries which show the highest profits in this country are foreign owned and make the least contribution to research and development.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE IN INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE IN INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
If we had a proper research and development program we would not have the unemployment problem or the inflation problem we have in this country. For example, Mr. Pocock, who was research director of the Lamontagne Senate Committee on Research and Development, suggested that if Canada had a research and development figure of 1.5 per cent of the gross national product in 1978,-and assuming that in order to reach that figure, 85 per cent of it would have come from the private industry-there would have been an extra
October 31, 1980

10,600 jobs for scientists and engineers, we would have had a total of 1.52 million new jobs created in the new industrial activities, and we would have had an extra $15.4 billion in exports. It would have solved our balance of payments problems and our unemployment problems.
Government studies have shown this, so why the inaction? Why not look at the obvious facts that all the highly paid mandarins and research people whom the government has hired have been telling it over all these years? Yet there has been no action, no results. Indeed, there has been a continuation of the 'do nothing' government. If anything, the Trudeau years will be remembered as the years when the essence of this country was drained, when the strength of this country was drained, making Canada more and more impotent.
There is nothing in the budget on how to deal with multinationals, how to force them to invest a decent amount of money in research and development in this country. There is talk, as there is always from across the benches. It is always being studied, it is always being considered. We have another committee, most probably a parliamentary committee or a royal commission, but no further action. There is talk about some tax incentives to industry. Already we have some very decent tax incentives for industry in order to encourage research and development, but they have not worked. The main reason is that the multinationals do not need them. They have access to cheap technology from their mother company and from their head office. The Canadian companies, the smaller businesses, which need it, very often do not have the income to benefit from the tax deductions.
What this party suggests is that more direct grants be made to Canadian industry and Canadian business and that the government and private industry make a deal, saying, "We will give you X amount of money to develop new technologies, provided that you guarantee that the jobs remain in this country." In other words, this party suggests that the government stop handing out the money, as they all too often do, and start making public money useful and working for the benefit of this country. All the money that has gone down the drain in this area, if used in an enlightened way, could have produced a much stronger research and development component in this country.
We object to tax incentives for research and development. I think there are wiser and better ways of doing it. Also, studies have shown that tax incentives will not work and have not worked in the past. It is shown as well that when you create tax incentives, essentially employment is created for lawyers and tax experts, and in too many cases employees, who would normally be doing other work in the company such as quality control, all at once are put on the payroll of the research and development section. In other words, there are too many loopholes and you do not achieve the desired affect.
We are suggesting, first, that direct grants be made to industries; and second, that we use a little bit of coercive power on the multinationals, in other words, that the government put into place an over-all tax and use that money in a special fund for research and development. Any company should be able to
Science and Technology
draw on that fund, provided again that they do the research and development in Canada and keep it here.
It is often asked: what can we do? We are such a small country, we just do not have the resources or the population base to produce effectively in this country a proper research and development component. Let me cite again from the research study by Mr. Pocock of the Lamontagne committee. He compared us with a group of countries which he called Norden-consisting of Norway, Sweden, Denmark and Finland-in 1975. The total population of the northern group was 27.4 million. Canada's population at the time was 23.3 million which was relatively comparable. They have the same topography, the same climate, and some of the same resources as we do here. Yet the industries in the Norden countries in 1975 spent $1.26 billion in U.S. dollars on research and development. What private industry in Canada spent at that time was only $681 million, roughly half of what was spent in those countries. The labour force employed in those countries in industry was some 33.4 per cent. Here it was only 26.6 per cent of our labour force. Smaller countries like Norway, Sweden and Denmark are able to do it. Why can we not do it here?

speechtext:
There is nothing in the budget which deals with how we will force the multinationals to do proper research and development in the country. The budget totally ignores the fact that any viable national economic strategy must emphasize two closely related objectives. The first would be the policies which must be formulated to channel capital and human resources together so that we can start tackling the technological problems this country faces, to channel capital and human resources together to bring business, labour, universities and government together to work out and develop coherent research and development policies and initiatives. Second, in order to fulfil the competitive requirements for improving Canada's industrial productivity, efficiency and employment, the federal government must through its policies vigorously promote the expansion of indigenous high technology manufacturing and the research efforts of our universities.
Specifically, the budget fails to address three key questions. What physical incentives are most likely to increase industrial research and development and technological innovation in Canada? How can government procurement be utilized more effectively to increase the demand for Canada's technology? How can we increase the export sales of Canadian made technology and reduce our traditional and very costly dependence on foreign imported technology?
I have been in touch with the Canadian Medical Research Council and it is very concerned about the implications of the
4314

Science and Technology
budget. The council would like to know if the government will adopt the medical research proposals for support of biomedical research in Canada, and if so, what level of support will the MRC receive, particularly in view of the proposed spending restraints in the social affairs envelope. There were some ominous noises by the Minister of Finance about the social affairs envelope. There were suggestions of moneys being saved.
Concerning the agreements with the provinces on cost-sharing, especially of higher education in the universities, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in 1976 promised that these programs were permanent, and if they were to be changed, they would only be changed subject to three years' notice. No three years' notice has been given, but it sounds from the budget as if these agreements will be changed and that the universities will end up with the short end of the stick. We cannot afford this any more. We have had too much of a brain drain already. Our universities are at the end of their ropes. They cannot continue with further cutbacks and slashes in their budgets. Young Canadians going into universities see no promise for employment at the end of the road. That is why they are now either not doing postgraduate studies, or are leaving the country. This drain must be stopped and stopped fast, if we are to meet the requirements five or ten years down the line, if we are to meet the requirements for trained people. The budget gives no assurances whatsoever that the drain will be stopped, that the government is prepared to tackle this problem and come up with some decent solutions. There is no hope in the budget at all. Throughout the universities across the country there is uncertainty.
It is not that we do not need trained people coming out of the universities. For example, 1 have been quite concerned with the whole area of pesticides and the testing thereof. Recently it has come to light that a number of the major American chemical testing firms that test our pesticides have deliberately falsified their results. There is a tremendous need for trained toxicologists in this particular field. I brought this matter to the attention of the government and they said, "Oh, no, we cannot do it. It will cost at least $8 million in core funding for the next five years; it is an impossible task". What a phony answer; what a phony answer!
There are decent programs throughout the country which are starving for funds. They are not asking for $8 million. Scientists at the University of Ottawa are trying to get a centre of toxicology together. They have their building, yet they have spent the last year or so scraping here and there for funding. They need some $30,000 to $40,000 to hire a director. There is no money for this, so the program is idle. It is not that we do not need toxicologists. Hundreds of new chemicals enter the market every year. We know a lot of these chemicals are not properly tested. We do not know what effects they are having on the health and welfare of Canadians. They must definitely be tested, yet the government opposite will not give the University of Ottawa some $30,000 to go on with the job of training toxicologists so that, five or six years down the road, there will be some trained toxicologists in the country
who can at least deal with the amount of chemicals entering the market. It is not that we will not pay the price. Of course we will pay the price. Every time there is Love Canal, or a thalidomide enters the market, somebody must pay. Generally it ends up that the government opposite is quite willing to hand out public funds to pay for mistakes, as it has done over and over again.
It is the insanity of the government opposite that it is not willing to spend a dollar today in order to save some $40 and $50 down the road. It is crazy thinking. It is thinking which arises because there is no coherent plan or policy. There is no coherent five-year projection in terms of what is needed and what is coming down the road. It is a government that reacts, reacts all the time.
I remember sitting in the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture when the estimates were before it. I indicated to the minister in charge that there were various new technologies coming down the road. I indicated that they would have a tremendous impact on the work force and on Canadian people generally. I asked him what was being done in order to direct this type of technological innovation and make certain that it benefited people rather than people simply reacting to it and it creating havoc in our society. The minister said-and I think it sums up the philosophy of the whole Liberal party and the Liberal government-"our role is not to initiate, our role is but to react". In other words, those particular technological innovations will come down the line, they will affect people, they will disrupt the work force and people's lives, and then the government will try to pick up the pieces. Surely in these times an ounce of prevention is what is needed.

I am reminded of a little verse by Melanie, who was one of the popular singers of the seventies. She had a very nice line, which was "You only pay a nickel, but you want a dollar song." That sums up the government opposite.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE IN INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the official opposition is, of course, very pleased to participate in the debate today on research and development. I would like to say debate, but perhaps the word "charade" would be more appropriate. We welcome any opportunity to prod, push and shove a reluctant government closer to the realization of the vital need to overhaul its attitude to research and development drastically and its priorities in spending and investing in technological upgrading.
I say investing rather than spending because there is a vast difference between spending massive amounts, multimillions of dollars on ongoing support programs, schemes and make-work situations, as opposed to heavily investing in legitimate job creation of an ongoing nature. By legitimate job-creating programs, I refer to those that result in lifelong career opportunities for young Canadians and long-term job opportunities for all Canadians in an industrial society which can take its place among the high technology, industrial societies of the world and not be gunned down by the Japanese, Germans, French and Americans, our industrial competitors who can out-produce us and undercut us in price and innovativeness.
Recent newspapers indicate the high priority that research is getting with such headlines as "Medical Researchers Issue Urgent Call for Funds", "Scientists Urged to Fight", "Ottawa Plans to Move Soon to Spur Research and Development", and "It's High Noon for High Technology". All these articles urge the government to get with it and develop our industrial capability. But what is happening to Canada today is what has been happening to Canada for years. This government has been warned for over a decade, by extremely knowledgeable and concerned scientists and industrialists, that our resource export strategy, if I could call it a strategy, unreinforced by higher technology processing, would cost us dearly in future years. At best we would become laminaters of wood and pumpers of water. That is one step up from the hewers of wood and drawers of water. One step up is about where we are.
Have you ever visited, Mr. Speaker, Upper Canada Village? Many Canadians visit Upper Canada Village each year to view the grain mills grinding wheat, the spinning wheels spinning yarn, and the saw mills cutting logs into rough boards. We go there to see how things were done in Canada 100 or 200 years ago. Things were simple and straightforward then, and we chuckle to ourselves and marvel at the slowness of the operations and the patience of the craftspeople of the day. We also recognize that such operations could not exist
and compete with the much faster and more efficient operations of today in milling, spinning, and lumber. But I wonder how many of us realize that if we walked into many of Canada's manufacturing plants today we would be looking at operations designed and carried on 50 or 100 years ago. Some of the equipment is bigger and faster, but the processes themselves are technologies of the past century. They are technologies which would be better passed on to Third World countries with their lower labour rates. Like the spinners and weavers of Upper Canada Village, these technologies are the slow and obsolete processes of the nineteenth century in a world which has almost passed out of the twentieth century.
And how do we get away with such obsolete planning and processing, backed up by obsolete government thinking? Why is there not a demand by Canadians for action to make Canada the most resource rich country in the world, the world leader in technology? Certainly Canada's scientists have spelled it out for us, both the pitfalls and the benefits.
It is very clear that Canadians do not realize that their high standard of living, bought with money raised through the sale of natural resources, is declining and will continue to decline as the world passes, in fact, rockets by us, with technological development of new products and processes which will make Canadian industry obsolete and deprive us of jobs.
Now this is not long-range future stuff. This is the stuff of the 1990s, the 1980s and even today. It is the provable, urgent message which industrialists, scientists, economists and researchers from all facets of Canadian industry have been telling this government for over a decade. To enjoy the benefits of higher technological manufacturing, you must be prepared to invest in research. From research comes design, invention, and innovation. From these come useful products and processes which will not only benefit Canadians through job creation, but which can be sold to other nations for other benefits. This means fewer imported goods, more exported goods; improved balance of payments for Canada, investment opportunities for Canadians, and career opportunities for young Canadians entering the work force. High technology companies do all these things. They have a higher rate of growth in employment than low research industries. They have higher productivity and they have annual price increases about half as great as those of low technology companies, so they benefit the consumers as well.
Knowing all these facts, what has the Trudeau government done about leading Canada forward through the decade of the seventies to world leadership in technology? Surely Canada's all-time biggest spender would be able to invest handsomely in vital research? For a man who claims to have a vision for Canada, perhaps a socialist one, but a vision nevertheless, surely his vision would include funding the most obvious and necessary component for national and social benefit, namely, research.
But instead, let us look at the record. In 1967 Canada invested 1.4 per cent of its gross national product in research
October 31, 1980

and development. In 1968 the new Trudeau government established a goal of 2 per cent GNP, definitely good news. But a decade later where has all the talk led us? We now have a new low of less than 1 per cent, .9 per cent to be exact, and we find ourselves on a par with other non-industrial nations like Ireland, Italy, and Iceland.
Now what is the government saying? The new minister of state for science, technology, environmental and constitutional affairs is once again talking sweet talk about new and high goals. By 1985, he says, we will be spending 1.5 per cent of GNP on research. But the federal government accounts for less than one third of total research spending in Canada. Provincial governments do some, but it is the private sector which must carry the load, and foreign firms, which used to do more research than Canadian firms, since 1975 do less. They are not treating us as sales opportunities for their foreign bases and they do not do research in Canada to a sufficient degree. How will the government encourage them or force them to do their fair share of research and grant world product mandate to Canada?
And even if we did reach 1.5 per cent by 1985, and I say to the minister we will not, where will that put us relative to our international competitors? Already our biggest competitor to the south is at 2.4 per cent. West Germany is at about 2.2 per cent, and Japan the world leader in technology is over 2 per cent and aiming to double that by 1985. So you see, Mr. Speaker, even if this government did reach its target-and 1 repeat that it will not-it will be too little and too late.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that the ill-fated Conservative government-by that I mean ill-fated for Canada-had set a target of 2.5 per cent research spending. With the serious commitment of government, backed by tax incentives, grants and strong government purchasing policies, that figure could be reached. It requires the understanding and the will of government to do it, not just to talk about it.
Take, for example, the massive contribution which research has made to the petroleum industry in enhanced recovery techniques. Instead of being able to extract about 20 per cent from an average oil well, we can now get about 35 per cent. It leaves a lot of oil in the ground, but it gets a lot more out, and all of that as a result of research. Think what that does for Canada's energy future, and think what such an increase in wealth accrues to Canada as a result of direct research.
Earlier I mentioned Japan's 1985 objective of 4 per cent research investing. Let us look at that country's progress over the past 35 years since its devastation by military defeat. Let me cite some examples given to a high technology conference here in Ottawa-a conference which, unfortunately, the minister did not attend-where 200 of the country's highest technology presidents and chief executives talked about the problems of technology in Canada. At that conference the minister might have learned something about the desperate need for technology in Canada. Mr. Walter Light, President of Northern Telecom, Canada's largest private research and development establishment, spoke at that conference. He is a man who, for years, has been trying to get this government to see
Science and Technology
the errors of its ways and its attitudes toward research. He gave us some very good examples of Japanese programs.
Japan, rising from the depths of almost total industrial devastation, is in the process of surpassing the United States as an industrial power. Think about that. Japan, a nation virtually without natural resources, a nation no bigger than the state of Montana and with only half the population of the U.S. is, because of determination and technological development, about to surpass the world's industrial leader.
Even though Japan's unionized labour costs have risen to par with those of the U.S., Japanese companies have consistently raised productivity and expanded their ability to produce quality products at the most competitive prices in the world, using our natural resources.
So, all you trade unionists in the NDP take note. We are selling our coal, steel, nickel and aluminum to Japan at an average price of about 50 cents a pound, and we are buying back Toyotas and Datsuns at about $3 a pound and more. It is that six, seven and eight times multiplier which is the job-creation program of the present government. That is what this government is doing in job creation. It is creating many jobs, jobs in Japan, Germany, Sweden and the United States. That is not just illogical, it is not just lack of direction and leadership, it is just plain stupid. It is bungling and inept government. It is a government which is selling Canada short.
Japan is now producing ten million cars annually, about 100 times what it produced 20 years ago and the equal of a good year in the United States.
What country do you think of, Mr. Speaker, when you think of precision tools and equipment, or watches? Switzerland, I suggest. Well, last year Japan produced ten million more watches than the Swiss. This is a classic example of how quickly a country can lose its world leadership if it ignores the new electronic technologies. The Japanese have long since overtaken and replaced the United States as the world leader in television and radio production. Japanese steel plants have the same capacity as the U.S. and almost as much as the entire European common market, and they are so technologically sophisticated that the U.S. uses Japanese standards as the base for measuring its trigger price for dumping.
In 1978, Japanese investment in new plant and equipment equalled that of the United States, but remember, with half the population the investment per capita was twice that of the U.S., and in the early 1980s it will surpass the U.S. in total research and development.
Very soon Japan will be a world leader in computers as it is in motorcycles, machine tools, copying machines, semi-conductors and even, perish the thought, snowmobiles.
What do we have to do to get this government to listen, to think and to discharge its duty and responsibility to lead Canada back into the technological age, to make Canada technologically competent, competitive, independent and capable of developing its own vast resources in order to sell

October 31, 1980
Science and Technology
finished products to the world and lower its dependence and vulnerability to world prices?
Will we forever maintain a back seat in the growth technologies of electronics and biotechnologies? These are not mysterious mumbo-jumbo words and unattainable objectives for a land such as Canada. They do not require large industrial complexes and vast populations. What they do call for is commitment; long-term, steady, determined commitment and large investments in money, as well as trained people and specialized industrialized resources. They are perfect for a resource rich, educated and skilled population such as Canada's.
In order to obtain large quantities of investment dollars, Canada should employ the same techniques it has used so effectively on frontier oil drilling and film making. Why should there not be a "super depletion" type of tax incentive for people willing to invest in high risk high technology companies just as in high risk drilling and high risk movie making? Certainly many films have recently been made in Canada, and not even this government could be so blind as to see the far greater benefits to Canada in having its citizens invest in high technology companies rather than in movie making.
Biotechnology is another new buzz word, a research field pregnant with possibilities for energy development, new manufacturing processes and greatly increased agricultural production. Canada should be getting in on the ground floor in order to enjoy the excellent returns just a few years down the road. Unlike unemployment insurance funds spent this year, next year and every year as an ongoing cost and burden to taxpayers of the future, biotechnology investment will return the money invested 20, 30 and 50-fold, while providing ongoing jobs to coming generations of Canadians.
Is this too much to ask of government? Is it too much to ask of the members opposite to take the time to acquaint themselves with the facts, the appalling record of Liberal government performance to date and the unquestioned opportunities which lie ahead, if we have the will and the resolve to grasp them? Well, regrettably, Mr. Speaker, it probably is too much to ask. This government is too involved with constitutional bickering, resource stealing and land grabbing, in between rounds of fighting with all the provinces and regions of Canada.
If we look at the record of the past Liberal decade we can read clearly of the decline of a once dynamic nation which could have had the world by the tail as far as economic prosperity is concerned. Instead, thanks to non-leadership, Canada is going backwards in technology, productivity, and relative standard of living. We are going upwards, boy are we going upwards, in government wasted spending, in annual deficits and in national indebtedness. All of these problems could be greatly aided by a serious effort to raise our level of technological competence.
We could start by having a full-time minister of science and technology, a full-time senior minister who understood, believed in, and would fight to convince a tired and
unimaginative cabinet of the desperate need for greatly increased funding of vitally needed research. The economic and social benefits to Canada would be just a few short years down the road, and they would be big benefits.
It is true they would come just too late to help this governm-nent survive the next election because research opportunities in Canada, when clearly plotted, show that a research company operates for five to eight years at a break even or loss position. However, the benefits beyond the eight years are clearly in the many times multiplier in profit generation for this nation.
If the government could see its way clear to fund past the next election, to give research and scientists a long-range opportunity to launch into these vitally needed long-term scientific projects, there would be great benefits down the road. While the government may not win the next election, it would certainly have the respect of the nation in that area, something which it does not have today.

speechtext:
I was going to say that if we are poetical, I could have characterized his speech as one of "sound and fury signifying nothing". I gather I cannot say that. While there was considerable sound, there was not much fury. I look forward to reading his speech in Hansard. I have already been told some of the details of it.
1 would say this to the hon. member, and to the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. Gilchrist). There is common ground among us. There is a recognition of the importance of the problems. There is no doubt about the need for the definition of a long-term science industrial policy. There is no doubt that the present commitments in gross national product terms of the Canadian economy, to the support of research and development, are inadequate. There is no doubt in my mind that the private sector-both opposition parties mentioned that the multinationals are not pulling their weight in the area of research and development, and that is true-the private sector is not doing as much as we think it should.
The problem is not the definition of the problem; the problem is whether we are acting and whether we are responding. It is in that area that I differ with the arguments put forward by my two hon. friends opposite. They say, "Let's look at the facts", and that is exactly what I want to do this afternoon-look at the facts to see how we are responding. As I said earlier, our response far outpaces that of our predecessors so briefly in office.
We are firmly committed to raising the level of research and development in Canada and to using science and technology in the furtherance of our social and economic objectives. The target we have set for ourselves is 1.5 per cent of the gross national product. The hon. member for Scarborough East said that his party's target was 2.5 per cent at the end of the decade. The critical path for reaching that target at the end of the decade is the same as the critical path for reaching 1.5 per cent by mid-decade. That is our objective.
In judging the success of our policy it seems to me that two fairly objective tests can be applied. The first is to ask what has been happening in the economy generally as it relates to research and development and, more particularly, to technology-intensive industries. The second is to ask what the government has done to encourage and support those developments.
Science and Technology
There is evidence to suggest that the downwind trend in research and development expenditures as a percentage of gross national product has been arrested.
The Financial Post in its recent special report on science and technology estimates that spending for research and development by major Canadian firms will increase 17.5 per cent this year compared to 1979. Between 1977 and 1980, the Financial Post, although its data is partial, found an increase of 33.6 per cent in research and development employment and a 91 per cent increase in spending for research and development.
Developments in a variety of aircraft sectors where high technology is important are very encouraging. In the aircraft section, employment in Canadair since 1975 has risen from 1,800 to 6,300 persons, sales from $37 million to $135 million, and there are 183 firm orders for the Challenger aircraft.
At de Havilland, sales have increased from $29 million to $280 million, and employment has risen from 2,700 to over 5,000 people. The Dash-7 has found a steady market.
The next generation of STOL aircraft-the Dash-8-is being developed, and there are already over 100 orders for it. The government is supporting and will support the development of the Dash-8.
In the space sector, which not so long ago was non-existent in Canada, employment now amounts to 2,500 and output to $140 million. Both of these areas are expected to grow over the next several years.
The creation of a whole new service industry dedicated to the provision of resource management data based on remote sensing via satellite has been created. This industry is spread right across the country from Newfoundland to Vancouver.
The Telidon program has led to the creation of a whole new service industry for the provision of information for the Telidon system. Companies such as Infomart and Hempton have invested more than $6 million in the research and development necessary to develop and market the data base essential to the Telidon concept. These companies are also beginning to achieve export sales of expertise. It has encouraged established electronics companies such as Microtel Pacific, Bell Canada, Electrohome, Norpak and SED to invest several million dollars in the expansion of their product lines to include Telidon hardware and software. It has helped Canadian cable system companies to get franchises in United States cities.
Telidon is being tested in Europe and the United States by such agencies as the Smithsonian Institute and the Public Broadcasting System. Over 150 new direct high technology jobs have been created already, and this is just the start. All of this has occurred with a government investment so far of about $5 million.
Recent surveys show a very high level of employment for applied scientists, engineers, technologists and technicians. For university and college graduates, the rate of employment of recent graduates is very close to 100 per cent in the applied fields of study including business, computer science, engineering, health, earth sciences, and the applied physical sciences.

Science and Technology
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, I would not claim for the government all the credit for the major trends and developments which I have mentioned and which are but a sampling of everything that is happening in this country in the field of high technology. But there is every reason to believe that the policies and programs of the government have had a generally beneficial influence and, in some case, a decisive one.
The remarks of the hon. member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong) this morning notwithstanding, tax incentives for industrial research and development have been successful. Canada has very generous measures compared to other OECD countries, and from what Statistics Canada and Revenue Canada have reported, compared to the United States. Canadian industry is taking good advantage of them. Our most recent data is for 1978, showing that 468 companies claimed research and development tax incentives whose total value we estimate to be about $28 million. Bear in mind that new tax incentives had only been introduced in 1977 and 1978, and industry was only beginning to respond at this point. A late 1978 tax incentive was also introduced but its effect does not show in these numbers, although 1 am confident it will have a significant impact. I expect that when the returns for 1979 and 1980 are available, the total claims will exceed $100 million.
I want to dwell on the expenditure side because the hon. member for Scarborough East denounced us for not acting strongly enough. I announced, on June 5 of this year, that the federal government expenditures on research and development in the natural sciences and engineering were slated to grow by 14 per cent over the previous year, an increase of $155 million. Since that time research and development spending plans have been approved for this year which will add a further $56 million to that total. I expect the year-over-year increase will be in excess of $200 million, representing an annual growth rate of more than 19 per cent. The hon. member accused me of using sweet words. That is flattering, I suppose, Mr. Speaker, but 19 per cent is much more than sweet words; it is action.
The 1980-81 increase of over 19 per cent shows that this government takes its commitment to the target very seriously and is prepared to put up its share of the target and to set the example for private industry, provincial governments and Canada's universities.
These expenditures, Mr. Speaker, cover a wide range of government activities. They include the mission-oriented research of departments such as the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, and the Department of the Environment. They include support for university research. And they include support for industry through agencies such as the National Research Council and departments such as the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Within this wide range of scientific activities I should like to point to some specific program increases-increases that effectively rebut the contention that we are not harnessing the energy and talents of our scientific and technological community.
I gather that the hon. member for Regina East who spoke this morning was critical of our efforts to help high technology
through the universities, with our funding for universities. He should know that among the increases included in the main estimates there is a major increase of $44 million for university support through the programs of the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council and the Medical Research Council, $30 million for industrial research and development support through the Enterprise Development Program of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, and $13 million for energy research and development.
With respect to the supplementary estimates which will shortly be placed before the House, these contain a further increase in research and development expenditures of approximately $47 million above the $1,242 million contained in the main estimates. Included in this increase are such items as $13 million for space science and satellite development; $17 million for industrial research and development under the Enterprise Development and DIP programs; $12 million for a low head hydroelectric demonstration; about $4.5 million for communications research and development, and $2 million for the Medical Research Council.
In addition to these increases, Mr. Speaker, it is anticipated that a further $9 million will be spent this year as part of the national energy plan presented in the House this week by my colleague, the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). As a consequence, the estimated expenditures on research and development by the government this year are now forecast at $1,298 billion, just under $1.3 billion, or 19 per cent higher than in 1979-80.
To some extent I apologize to hon. members for having gone on with statistics at such length, but the fact is that we should look at the facts, and the facts do not bear out the contentions of the two opposition members who have spoken before me.
Equally, I should draw the attention of hon. members to the research and development implications of the national energy program. That program fully recognized the importance of energy research and development in meeting our energy situation and the need to have more support for energy research and development measures at both the provincial and federal levels of government and in industry. Moreover, the program contains important new initiatives in research and development which will be undertaken to provide the technological base for long-term energy options.
The over-all research and development emphasis, however, must shift toward new energy priorities. The three priorities for this increased effort are, first, alternatives to gasoline as fuel; second, increased efficiency of energy use in all sectors of the economy; and third, new energy sources ranging from coal to hydrogen. In this regard the federal government will undertake new energy research and development initiatives totalling $260 million over the period 1980 to 1983. This will be a significant commitment in energy research and development expenditures in addition to the $160 million spent in 1979-80 under the panel on energy research and development.
October 31, 1980

The government has a genuine concern about large-scale and efficient energy development in Canada. Yesterday the government announced the creation of a new Crown corporation, Enertech Canada, to enhance further Canada's energy position by giving a boost to renewable energy development. Enertech will operate under the guidance of Petro-Canada initially and will incorporate the Solar Energy Society of Canada and the Biomass Energy Institute. Petro-Canada will provide initial funding of $20 million to Enertech, which will be located at Winnipeg.
Canada is rich in a variety of energy resources. More and more emphasis will be placed on renewable energy resources and on public education to appreciate and wisely use this important national asset.
The government considers the large intellectual resource base within our universities as a major and basic building block of any vigorous and soundly based industrial policy. That is one of the main reasons why the government has increased the budget of NSERC by 35 per cent this year.
