We greatly increased it, and we did so because we are intent on ensuring that the council is able to attract and train more young, high calibre talent for research careers in Canada.
The council has provided some 1,000 awards to third and fourth-year undergraduates for summer jobs in research, and 100 new senior research fellowships. This latter program has brought highly experienced researchers back to Canada from abroad.
The council has directed an increasing proportion of university research and development into areas of national need. Its strategic grants program has stimulated research in energy, environmental toxicology, oceans, communications, and food and agriculture. Particular priority in those programs is given to the transfer of research results to industry.
The government is also sponsoring new industrial innovation centres at the Ecole Polytechnique and at the University of Waterloo. These centres will aid industry, particularly small business and inventors, in the development of new products.
1 have described the ways in which we have harnassed-and harnassed effectively-the energy and talents of our scientific and technological community. I have pointed to a number of developments taking place across the country which have moved Canada into the forefront of international developments in space, in communications, in aeronautics, in electronics, and in energy, to name only a few.
Science and Technology
Some of these developments have taken place entirely in the private sector; others have been fostered or encouraged by the federal government. All are not only contributing now to our economic growth but they are also laying the groundwork for a healthy, competitive and high technology economy in the future.
I have also pointed to some of the key developments taking place in government. We have fixed a research and development target of 1.5 per cent of gross national product, including both public and private sector spending, as the objective for the research expenditures of our economy by the mid-eighties. We fully expect to meet what we feel is a reasonable share of that target this year. We are on track toward meeting that target. I am hopeful that we will do the same next year. The additional resources which we have received have enabled us to provide selective increases in some government research through the granting councils, and additional support for research and development in industry. That pattern embodies the main elements of our approach. They are maintaining a healthy scientific capability with government departments and agencies to permit them to carry out their missions, undertaking the kind of research which cannot readily be done in the private sector, or it is too expensive to be done in the private sector, or the returns are too long-term to be done easily within the private sector.
Our approach includes providing assistance to research at the university level, trying to ensure that curiosity oriented research will be supported, and training and developing in human resources the capacity to meet our objectives. Basically that support flows through the granting councils to ensure, among other things, as I have said, a flow of highly trained individuals to support science and research. Finally, our approach includes providing increased support directly and indirectly to industry, which clearly has a major role to play. We are counting upon greatly increased expenditures in the private sector to bring us to the 1.5 per cent objective.
These elements are in place, and the essence of my remarks this afternoon is that, contrary to the assertions of hon. gentlemen opposite, we are making considerable progress. We are devoting increased resources to these efforts, and we are moving in the right direction.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to take part in this debate. I want to try to broaden the look at the problem just a little bit and to take it from the research and development area just a little further into the entire area of industrial strategy, because I think it is important that we take a look at what is happening to Canada and what is happening to our industry and the value that we will hopefully derive from the kind of program my colleague, the hon. member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong), put forward if in fact the government were ever to get around to adopting that kind of program.
I listened with interest to the minister as he outlined the number of projects, project areas and companies involved in research and development of one kind or another and, without getting into a battle of semantics, there is the question of

whether they are doing pure research or product research, or in fact in many instances market research.
There are serious questions in that regard, and I think that in order to break it down it might be useful to have a breakdown of the statistics to show where the research was done and what kind of research is being done. However, 1 am not going to play the game of trading in statistics. I will not do so because 1 think that the measure of the government's success is not whether 1 can come up with a statistic which shows that it is spending less, or the government can come up with a statistic which shows that it is spending more. The measure of government success can be found in the unemployment figures which come out every week and which show dramatic increases. The measure of the government's success can be found in the bankruptcy courts as more and more small industries, small companies, and not so small companies, are being faced with situations in which they are no longer competitive in world terms for one reason or another, or they are unable to meet their commitments because of an economy which has been allowed to get out of hand, and costs which are too large for them to bear.
The measure of success can be found in family courts as people try to find solutions to purely personal problems which are the direct result of the government's failure to move to rationalize this economy and come to grips with the problem areas.
It can be found in the social welfare offices as people who have been unemployed and looking for work, any kind of work, in almost every community all across the country, finally find themselves with no unemployment insurance benefits and forced to do what they in their own minds thought they would never have to do, and that is to go down to the welfare office to ask for help.
So I do not think that you can measure the success, in terms of the definition of the new economic strategy or the new industrial strategy, the appropriateness of the amounts made available for research and development, in statistics, not in financial statistics anyway. I think they can be found in human experiences, young people who walk out of universities or community colleges, young people who come out of high schools with diplomas which, not so many years ago, meant something, diplomas which gave them a reason to believe that there would be something for them if they applied themselves, young people who walk out today with a diploma in their hand and wonder what it is worth, where do they go, what value does it have.
The other night I listened as the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) explained to the House of Commons and to the nation the government's new approach to managing the economy of Canada, and I could not help thinking how wrong-headed it was, how this approach can do nothing but be counterproductive, and how this approach can do nothing but create more of the same kinds of problems with which we have been confronted over the course of the last half dozen years. What
the Minister of Finance did was to make it more expensive to do business in Canada. What the Minister of Finance did was to make it more expensive to provide the essential things for your family. What the Minister of Finance did was to reduce the amount of discretionary income for the majority of people. What he did, in fact, was to undermine an already imperilled economic sector by adding to the burden, a burden which even now is almost unbearable.
1 want to suggest today that it is, therefore, not easy to talk about industrial strategy without talking about the budgetary measures that must be put in place in order for this industrial strategy to have any meaning, to have any direction, to have any substance. What the Minister of Finance did was to say that much of what people are talking about, in terms of a new and dynamic Canada with a changed economy, a new manufacturing sector, new and better means of better production, could not be achieved. What he did in that budget was to determine effectively that our manufacturing sector would not be able to undergo the massive change that would have to be undergone if we are going to be competitive in this world's marketplaces.
Canadian industry is, in the main, quite small. It was set up for the purpose of meeting the domestic market of eight million or nine million households, and that is not a very large market. This means, therefore, that if the Canadian industry, small in scale as it is, is going to be successful, it has to be both very efficient and also be able to rely on a stable domestic market as the basis for its growth, so that it can then, with that sense of stability, go out into the world and seek the world's markets and thereby take advantage of additional dollars to provide for Canadians opportunities which until now have not been provided.
I want to suggest to you that if you were to stop and analyse this budget, you would have to come to the conclusion that the discussion we are having today, important though it is, pales into insignificance when you realize that all the goals and the directions we are trying to achieve are being undermined. They are being undermined by the actions of the financial advisers to the government. God knows why. I cannot understand it at all. I sat for two days puzzling, trying to see the rationale.
Here we are with resources in abundance; you name it, we have it. Here we are with natural resources, depletable and non-depletable, with energy resources sufficient to meet our needs if properly used, with manufacturing capacity and an infrastructure in place, although desperately needing to be updated, with perhaps the most highly educated work force in the world, with the ability to produce our own food, with a stable banking system, with stability in government, except for the last few years. And yet we have to ask ourselves what it is that we do not have, what is holding us back, why are we not in the forefront, why do we look to Japan, to Germany, to other parts of the world with envy when they have to come to us to get the very things they need? Why do we have to look to them? One of the reasons is the kind of budgetary measures that were brought in this week and that are not too much

October 31, 1980

unlike the kind of budgetary measures that were brought in last year by the Conservative government.
If you reduce the number of discretionary dollars available in the consumer marketplace, that can do nothing other than reduce the amount of purchasing that will take place. If you reduce the amount of purchasing that will take place, it automatically follows that you will reduce the number of products required to be manufactured, and if you reduce the number of products required to be manufactured, you will no doubt reduce the number of people required to manufacture the products, and they will be unemployed.
If you create more unemployment, you will have fewer people paying taxes, and as you have fewer people paying taxes, those who are paying taxes will have to pay more, and as those paying taxes have to pay more, you will begin again the cycle because they will not have as many discretionary dollars, and the manufacturers who are desperately seeking ways to improve their productivity, to build up their manufacturing capacity, and to embark on product line research and pure research necessary to be competitive, not only in Canada but in the world, will not have a sufficient cash flow to put aside the dollars they must have in order to do the research, in order to undertake the engineering, and in order to do the work. Therefore, the whole process becomes self-defeating, and then becomes a major problem because it becomes in itself a destructive process.
It amazed me, therefore, when I listened to the government speaking, and remembered the time when the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray)-he is now in Paris, as I understand it, and I hope he is enjoying himself- God, I am glad he is not here.

million. That is a way of measuring the commitment of the government and deciding whether the country is in good hands with or without Allstate.
In essence what I am saying is that we have a problem not unlike those faced by many other nations in the world, but in Canada we have a different approach. But imports are up 148 per cent, and that looks terrible. In end products in Ontario exports in the same period are up 2 per cent but imports are up 18 per cent. This reflects a weakness in

our manufacturing sector, in our ability to meet the world demand, in our ability to utilize research and development capacity and in our ability to be competitive. Ontario faces extremely difficult times, and we still do not have in place any kind of strategy to deal with it.
I gather from the eagerness with which Mr. Speaker sits on the edge of his chair that I have reached a point where I should stop, but 1 want to say that the kinds of measures being proposed are not really good enough. In fact, they are counterproductive. The government had better get up off its collective butt and do something before there is no country left to save.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE IN INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 am very happy to take part in this debate this afternoon on the motion presented by the New Democratic Party. Its justification for any changes in economic policy or anything it ever suggests is that there is a strategy written somewhere. Because some thesis is written in a university or in the caucus research bureau of the NDP, it becomes a proposal of that party. It suggests that whatever needs to be done to prop up industrial sectors of the economy can be done in Parliament just because a group of politicians in Ottawa decides to do something which they believe will automatically solve every industrial development problem in the country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE IN INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext: Who said that?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE IN INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
The member should read his own motion to which he did not refer when he made his speech. When one looks at the motion, listens to the speeches members over there made today and the ones they made in the budget debate, as well as other speeches made before, one draws that conclusion. I am not suggesting they are being dishonest or insincere. They just do not know any better. They believe it is possible for the government to do everything. They begin with their political aspirations and believe it is possible to repair everything that is wrong in the Canadian economy. That is just not the way it works.
It was interesting to hear a spokesman of the Conservative party earlier today advocating more government spending as a way of solving problems in the industrial sectors of the country. That party, whenever they had a chance to govern-thank God it did not last very long-immediately went on a rampage to cut every possible productive program which the federal government had. I see the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) is in the House. He must recall the humiliation he went through last year at about this time because the president of the treasury board at that time had cut back on every good program there was, including those in the Department of Fisheries. Of course he disagreed with that but there was not much he could do. The collective ideology of the Conservative party took priority. So to hear somebody from the Conservative party advocating more spending in order to prop up more research in our industrial sectors is really funny to somebody who sits on this side of the House. Last year, for a period of a few months, we saw them slash every possible program which was productive. I say, "Thank God it didn't last very long". Now we are back in power. We won the
election in February, and a lot of those programs are back onstream. They will help to develop sectors in the economy which are important and have a positive impact on people. The fisheries sector is one of these programs.

Now when members come out and say there are bankruptcies in the economy, lay-offs and some slow-downs they blame it on the fact that the government does not have another program. It is an indication that they are either not being honest with themselves or the House or that they do not understand any better. There is an awful lot of innovation happening in the economy now. Some of it is helped by government and sometimes it is helped through the taxation system. We have investment tax credits in place particularly for research and development. When some hon. members speak about the budget which was tabled this week they say every possible negative thing they can about it; they do not look at its positive aspects. The New Democratic Party does not look into certain designated areas of the country where there is a more urgent need for industrial development. For these areas we have provided a special investment tax credit of 50 per cent. The hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) shakes his head. He referred to the investment of Michelin as a handout when he spoke earlier.

speechtext: That is exactly what it is.

Because Michelin happens to create competition in his area-they are a very aggressive company who go for the best products in the world, not only in Canada-

It is going to defeat you in the next election.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE IN INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member should address his remarks to the Chair.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE IN INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
I was addressing my remarks to the Chair, Mr. Speaker. I was saying to you, sir, that I do not mind those interjections. As a matter of fact, they do not make any more sense than when the hon. member is on his feet making a speech, so I have no problem in responding to them. He has been here for a little while and he has many shortcomings in proposing all sorts of programs. He says we should do this for the auto industry and we should do that for the other industries. In some cases he is right. The government should be attentive to some of those problems. But then when the government does do something which is productive and positive, he ridicules it, he says it is just a handout to Michelin or a handout to another company. He has to make up his mind and when he does his speeches will be a little more coherent.
Mr. Speaker, the NDP talk about an industrial strategy as if, in a country like Canada, you could have a blueprint, a strategy written somewhere by bureaucrats, academics or theoreticians. He seems to think something like that is possible in a country where there are at least five different economies-some people think there are even more different economies than that. At one end of the country we have a shortage of workers and at the other there is between 15 and 20 per cent unemployment. In some parts of the country we depend on resources only and in other parts we have a very productive manufacturing sector. There just cannot be a blueprint which will be adaptable to the whole country when there are these kinds of diverse economies. I can give some examples.

Mr. Speaker, here is an example of something which occurred in New Brunswick a few years ago. Everyone knows that the Saskatchewan government took special action concerning the potash industry, probably in the interest of the province, and I make no judgment on this issue. The authorities decided to get tougher with the companies and said: You will have to do certain things for the good of Saskatchewan, or else we shall take over these companies. In some cases, they did so. On the other hand, in New Brunswick, which also has a potash industry, the government decided not to follow the same development strategy nor to apply the same criteria as the Saskatchewan government because it wanted to see development in this area. Could the federal government and all the provincial governments agree on a strategy for potash development in this case? This would be impossible because one area would say that it prefers to have development under
Science and Technology
such terms or such conditions, while another area has decided that it does not want the same things. 1 respect these decisions. I make no judgment about this matter. It is up to the Saskatchewan government, with the people of the province, to decide what type of development policy it wants to apply.
In my constituency near Bathurst, for instance, there is a zinc mine and several other mines which are amongst the most productive in North America and probably the world and which belong to Brunswick Mining & Smelting. This is now a subsidiary of Noranda Mines Limited. At the present time, there is a zinc refinery, and in the last few years, the federal government and the government of New Brunswick have been trying through all sorts of incentives to help this company. The tax credit of 50 per cent announced Tuesday night by the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) will apply to this area, and it might very well encourage the company to build a second zinc refinery. Moreover, under the programs of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and the agreement concerning northeastern New Brunswick, there are other means through which the federal government could contribute to this project.
But ten years ago, if we had had taken a leaf out of the New Democratic Party's book, if we had said we needed an industrial strategy in Canada, someone somewhere must draft a paper that says it will be a coherent policy, coherent is a nice word, we would probably have said: Canada as a whole must ensure that resources be processed right where they are taken out of the ground. That is one of the objectives of the federal government. That is the objective that has been followed in the case of uranium, for instance, when it was said that the refinery would be established in northern Ontario, very close to the uranium mines.
We can say that in some areas of the country, but if that was what had been said in my area some seven or eight years ago, the mine would be closed. Economically, the company had no reason to build a second refinery at that time, because opening the mine required the conclusion of an investment agreement with people who owned refineries in Belgium and used to get their supply from mines in the Congo when the Congo belonged to Belgium. So then we would have had to close the mine if we had wanted to follow the national strategy, which would have meant that the 1,800 people who have been working there since would have been unemployed. Therefore a national strategy is not possible, unless we say we are going to draft a national strategy, be dishonest and not follow it.
A country such as Canada needs sectorial and regional industrial development policies, and the same applies to the provinces themselves. It is impossible to have what might be called a coherent policy or strategy unless one was dishonest and outlined such a strategy which would simply set goals for the whole country, and then failed to pursue them. So, Mr. Speaker, 1 would rather be honest with the people and tell them that what we need are sectorial regional policies.

October 31, 1980
Science and Technology
To pretend like the Conservative member and the NDP member that the federal government has not been very active or enterprising, even with respect to regional development policies in the past 12 to 15 years, is to ignore the situation. I understand that the member is a newcomer from the Ontario legislature; that he is not used to sitting in the House of Commons, but if he cares to ask members who have been sitting here longer than him, such as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), that member will be able to tell him that the federal government has had regional development policies for a long time and that they are sectorial and promote development in various areas of the country. There are examples, and I just gave one, Michelin Tires, there are some in my own riding. There is a corporation-
1 observe that the hon. member does not listen when I give examples. Another example is a company in my constituency called SMI Industries which makes snowplow equipment, snow-clearing equipment, crash rescue trucks and the Zam-boni ice machines which are sold all over the world. This was only possible through federal-provincial development policies. It was only possible because this government has departments such as DREE, Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Department of Transport. These departments were interested in making sure that that particular sector became equal with the best in the world. It was all done by government encouragement through incentive programs.
Because there is no written document called an industrial strategy, it does not mean there is no industrial strategy. Perhaps the researcher who helps the hon. member would, from an academic point of view, like to see everything written down like a thesis. I do not suggest that the hon. member uses a researcher all the time.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE IN INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext: Don't get sidetracked, finish your speech.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE IN INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext: I am suggesting that it is possible to approach these problems from an academic point of view rather than from a practical point of view.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE IN INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE IN INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext: The hon. member talks about real people, but his party has been advocating an industrial strategy for Canada for some time.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE IN INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext: So has Herb Gray.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE IN INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext: The NDP say that because there is no document or piece of paper on which is written our industrial strategy, it means nothing is being done to promote industrial development in the country. What I am saying is that we have policies which are sectoral and regional in nature and which promote industrial development in this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE IN INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext: We'll talk again.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE IN INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
Sure, we will talk again.

So, Mr. Speaker, coming back to the budget which was introduced on Tuesday, for the Maritime provinces, for areas in my constituency, it is a favourable budget because we are in an area which depends to a large extent on the power the federal government will have to develop not only energy but the whole Canadian economy. Because all eastern Canada, all the province of New Brunswick for instance, depends on a strong federal government and the federal government can only be strong if it retains a major part of the revenues produced by the economy of Canada. Unless the federal government has enough money it is no use saying that it will be strong enough to take care of the welfare of all Canadians, and that it will be able to deal with the interests and the economic development of the weakest parts of our country.
For my region it is important to emphasize that the philosophy underlying the government budget is favourable to us. In addition, the government is not following a fiscal policy which might be described as being regressive because it does not seek to slash overly drastically into government projects. So our region will be able to continue to progress without being subjected to a direct impact which might be disastrous because, when the federal government cuts expenditures, it means that regions whose growth depends on the federal government will suffer a lot more than other regions which have less urgent need for these expenditures. Then there is the fact that oil prices will not go up as rapidly as they would have if the December budget of the Progressive Conservatives had been adopted. Indeed, between now and 1984 there will be a striking difference between what the price of petroleum would have been under the Conservative budget of December and what it will be under the budget presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) on Tuesday. In fact, according to the Tory budget the price of gasoline would have been SI.56 in 1981 and, I conclude on this, Mr. Speaker, $2.63 in 1984, against $1.36 in 1981 and $1.95 in 1984 as provided in the budget we are now considering. So there is a difference of 60 cents a gallon in the price of gasoline, not to mention the 18-cent excise tax which the Progressive Conservatives were suggesting last year.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would say that the government is introducing dynamic, active and positive measures in the field of industrial development and, in my opinion, the budget unveiled last Tuesday evening faithfully reflects that philosophy and that approach of the government, and that they will continue, I am sure, to meet the requirements of the regions which need them.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE IN INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not with pleasure, but with discomfort that I rise to
October 31, 1980

support my colleagues on this side of the House, including those in the NDP, who put this motion forward condemning the government for having failed to harness the energies and talents of Canada's scientific and technological community. I say it is with some discomfort because 1 have heard two speakers from the opposite side, most recently the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau), using slick rhetoric and simple examples, picked selectively, to make a case which is very, very difficult to defend.
I would like to put a couple of over-all figures on the record which members of the government have failed to address. The minister's departmental estimates for this year show that for science and technology the government will spend, over all, $400 million this year. That compares with a budget of $577 million for the CBC and with a budget of $2.3 billion for the operation of the Department of the Secretary of State. Science and technology is receiving 20 per cent as much attention as the Department of the Secretary of State. In fact the total science and technology research effort in Canada consumes about $2.3 billion out of a gross national product of $250 billion, or less than 1 per cent. That $2.3 billion spent by all industry and all governments in Canada is the same as the budget for the Department of the Secretary of State of this government.
I believe that this is atrocious. The future opportunity for our children, as they grow up, will depend primarily on jobs created by the technological advancement of our country. I speak with some authority on this matter because I grew up in a small prairie town in Alberta, and I make no apologies for that. We were without paved roads, natural gas and many of the conveniences which those who were raised in this more affluent, central part of Canada have enjoyed for decades.
My parents wanted to see that I got an education. They did everything to ensure that I got that education. They even went so far as to sacrifice a family car so that my brothers, sisters and I could have an education. I found a way to work for that education. I went to the University of Alberta where I studied mechanical engineering and to the University of Toronto where I studied aerospace engineering. I spent nine years in university obtaining advanced degrees to put myself in a position where I could be employed in a high technology area in this country. Then I looked around for a job. I had the choice of five jobs in the United States of America at 60 per cent higher salary than would be offered in Canada, where there were few jobs in the private sector in aerospace industries. I had the alternative of going into a Canadian university, to teach which I did, in 1969, at a much lower salary. I felt the future of this country was important. Teaching in that university and in my work over ten years I built a research program. I used the benefits of the National Research Council and the other aid programs of this country. However, I found to my great distress that the greatest support for my research effort came from American companies to whom I also provided consulting services. These were companies such as General Electric, General Motors, Douglas and Grumman. Those companies were willing to invest in the work I was doing in
Science and Technology
Canada at magnitudes five times as large as the Canadian government was willing to provide. Over that ten-year period at the University of British Columbia, the relative amount of money available for research was gradually in decline because of the policies of the government. This government has been under the leadership of one Prime Minister for 11 years. It has allowed research and development to deteriorate to a criminal state in Canada. I found that the graduate students that I trained had to leave Canada. Some of them are working in California today. There was no private sector opportunity for them in Canada upon their graduation.
I found I had to go to the United States for research contracts and support, and that there were no Canadian industries particularly interested in hiring the products of our program. In spite of the high-sounding rhetoric from former ministers of state for science and technology I must say that, as a consequence of the Lamontagne committee report of the early 1970s, the government has perpetrated the greatest charade of all times on this country by establishing a ministry of state for science and technology which is absolutely toothless.
I want to give some examples to illustrate that contention. I am here today helping to preside over the collapse of our scientific and technological base. I hope it will not collapse. But from what I have seen and heard from the minister today,
I am afraid that is the direction in which this country is going.
I want to read a letter from a former colleague of mine at the University of British Columbia. It is a letter to the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Roberts) written in September, 1980. This individual is a plasma scientist. He has been active in Canada for many years working on fusion research and plasma research. He now sits on the selection committee for the National Science and Engineering Research Council grants committee on energy. This gentleman said in his letter:
I attended my first meeting recently and came to realize that the resources of this agency,-
The agency he is referring to is the selection committee.
-are insufficient to maintain the fusion research of this country at its present awareness level, let alone raise it to a level comparable to other developed countries of similar size.
He went on to say:
Research and development for fusion energy requires a long lead time but it probably has a huge energy pay-off.
He continued:
The question comes down to this: Does Canada want to forfeit its hold on research in fusion, squander its expertise in the field and isolate itself from the technology which may provide the only inexhaustible and acceptable energy source in the long run? This question must be faced immediately and is far too important to be answered by default.
He says that he is faced with a choice and that physics researchers in Canada are faced with the choice of getting out of fusion research because Canada is not prepared to keep the fusion energy option open for the next generation.

October 31, 1980
Science and Technology
That is only one of the selective examples I will use today. There are many others.
Forestry research in this country enjoys the grand sum of $30 million of support. That product returns $18 billion to the people of Canada. So the sum I mentioned is less than 0.2 per cent of the value of that product. That is all this government is willing to reinvest in the area of science and technology. Total spending on forestry, including reforestation by provincial and federal governments, is somewhat less than 1 per cent of the $18 billion which that product returns to the nation much of which comes from my province of British Columbia.
I would like to put on record some other gross figures which are astonishing and appalling in their impact. I am quoting from a MOSST report of 1978. It is known that industries in other industrial countries are more heavily supported in research costs by their respective governments. In the United States, the U.S. government foots the bill for 37 per cent of research costs. In Canada the figure is 11 per cent, only one-third as much, and that is appalling.
In terms of percentage of research and development activity, we find that total expenditures on R and D in Canada are at the present time a little more than 0.9 per cent of GNP-that is, less than 1 per cent. By comparison, in Switzerland the figure is 2.2 per cent; in Germany 2.1 per cent, and in the United States 2.3 per cent. Canada is heading into an intellectual tomb if we keep this up. Expenditures by sector of performance show that in Canada business puts up only 40 per cent of the investment in research and the government puts up more, whereas in Germany business puts up 66 per cent. The private sector is somehow induced to put 60 per cent more of its revenue into research than is being done in Canada. Switzerland, the United States and Sweden all have more than 70 per cent of the revenue in research coming from the private sector. In Canada that figure is only 40 per cent. We are top-heavy in industrial laboratories and university establishments and far too light in the area of industrial research dollars.
I have one final figure. This deals with the number of Canadians employed in research per 1,000 persons employed. In Canada, 3.5 Canadians in every 1,000 are employed in research and development. In the United Kingdom the figure is 10 persons per 1,000. In Sweden the figure is 8.4 persons per 1,000; in France the figure is 7.5 persons per 1,000 and in Germany, 9.5 persons per 1,000.
We cannot have this minister standing hypocritically opposite telling us that everything is well in Canada, whereas in fact he is spending his time travelling to see the Queen and giving speeches prepared by bureaucrats to conferences and offending the scientific community. I know that for a fact, and in a few moments I will read for the record some of the choice selections from a recent speech he has given. He is not even here in the House; he does not have the courtesy to stay this afternoon for the rest of this debate.
In our short term in office, and under the leadership of the hon. former member for Brome-Mississquoi, the Conservative government took a number of positive initiatives. I will not sit here and hear the present Minister of State for Science and
Technology (Mr. Roberts) trying to take credit for a substantial increase in funding to the universities of Canada, because this was an initiative of our government under the leadership of that member from Brome-Mississquoi. Last November he announced an increase of some 33 per cent-some $40 million annually-of funding to research and development through the science and engineering research council. That amount is shown in this government's very estimates. It is an increase to a level of support of $160 million which was approved by our cabinet and our government, and they stand over there and attempt to take credit for it.
The Conservative government also approved the five-year plan which the present minister talks a lot about. It also commissioned and received the report on "opportunities for Canadian research and development directed toward the needs of the North American auto market". These are specific initiatives compared with the gobbledygook we get from the present minister, as reflected in his speech which he gave on October 21, 1980, to the first Canadian conference on astronautics. That, in a way of speaking, is my alma mater because that is the profession in which I was trained. The minister went before those scholarly gentlemen, well trained at the expense of the Canadian taxpayer and told them that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) had given him two very important tasks. First of all, he had been given the responsibility for space R and D, the first time a single minister had been given this role. His second important task was to aid in implementing the government's policy mandate, he says he is now responsible for co-ordinating all of the government's space activities. The minister then listed off a whole series of programs and studies that he was supposed to embark upon given those first steps. It is more programs, more talk, but no action. That is the record of this government over the past ten years which has brought this country to its knees in technological advancement.
I could get more incensed, but I will move to a slightly less intensive topic. I want to talk for a few moments about the federal budget. There is nothing in this budget for science and technology. There is only more deficit. In fact, there is $4 billion more deficit than we projected when the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) presented his budget last December. If we are even going to get Canada up to the level of 1 Zi per cent of GNP in research and development, let alone 2Vi per cent, we will need to get over a billion dollars injected into research and technology in this country, right now. There were not even any scraps in the budget to come anywhere close to the billion dollar injection we need.
There were no tax policies which would encourage Canadian research investment by Canadian industries; no policies on foreign investment, including the implementation of world product mandates, and no incentives for foreign companies to reinvest a portion of their earnings in research and development in Canada, building laboratories and providing employment opportunities in this country. There was no direct injection of capital to serve the needs of industry and our universities. There was no recognition of the fact that the
October 31, 1980

moneys which universities have available for the pure sciences, engineering and social sciences, and medical science, is way out of proportion to what is required. Canada is slipping ever further into the levels of effort characteristic of Third World countries.
I wish to read a couple of quotations with regard to the budget-statements made by representatives of the high technology industry. They appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of Wednesday, October 29, under the heading "High Technology Industry Angry". I am angry too, Mr. Speaker, I quote:
Spokesmen for Canada's fledgling high-technology industry reacted with anger and frustration Tuesday night after learning that the federal budget contained virtually nothing to help them catch up with the rest of the world ... Canada, spending less than one per cent of the gross national product (GNP) on research and development, is already lagging behind almost all other industrialized countries-and the gap is growing.
"All these other countries have some sort of an industrial game plan," said Robert Long, executive director of the Canadian Advanced Technology Association, which represents 78 companies.
Jack Davies, president of Ottawa's Systemhouse Ltd., a computer consulting firm, said:
"It's truly a Canadian problem that the government just cannot see the inventiveness, the creativity and the technical ability of the people in this country," said a disappointed Davies-
"The government is nervous, so basically they've decided to do nothing for now," said Larry Clarke, chairman of Spar Aerospace in Toronto.
"But I get concerned as time passes because it's very expensive to stay on the treadmill."
There are thousands of opportunities in this country from which this government is abdicating. We have a quarter of a million dollar noise-monitoring system at Toronto international airport which does not work. Some bureaucrat went to Texas, was wined and dined, and decided an American company should get the contract even though four Canadian scientific firms put in competitive bids. That is not right.
We have satellite antenna receiving equipment being manufactured in this country and the Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox) is going around taking them down; this is equipment manufactured by Canadian technological firms. If he is not prepared to change the law to give people the right to freedom of speech and freedom of the press, then our country is headed for censorship and utter disaster. We are destroying our own technological and electronic industry by not allowing Canadian firms to manufacture these receiving stations and to sell them for use by Canadians.
1 have seen applications for research projects, such as using crushed wood fibres to build a substitute for plywood, turned down by the Department of the Environment, the Department of Supply and Services and the Minister for Science and Technology. They did not want to take a $200,000 risk on a project conducted by Canadians who knew their business.
Fusion technology is something to which this government is oblivious. A gentleman in Winnipeg has designed a new automotive cycle called the K-engine cycle, i am a technical person and I say that that cycle may have tremendous benefits in potential energy savings. It has a potential to produce a whole new industry for Canada which the government has
Science and Technology
neglected. There is also a potential particularly attractive in the province of Quebec to manufacture electric cars for commuter use and sell them to every city in North America. Who is picking up the ball? We are certainly not getting any leadership from this government.
Getting back to the budget, we are destroying the incentives of the energy industry. We are driving billions of investment dollars out of this country. That is going to mean lost jobs for our young people and lost opportunities in the future. Now we are going to nationalize the oil industry, or 25 per cent of it. What will happen to the auto industry? Are they going to get nervous next? If the government intends to nationalize the oil industry, why not nationalize General Motors, Safeway Stores, IBM, Xerox and General Electric? This government is destroying the instinct of the private sector and the freedom it has always enjoyed in this country to advance and prosper and employ our young people in jobs which are rewarding, and which allow them to earn in proportion to their individual efforts.
Now there is to be another Crown corporation to add to the list of some 440. We are to have Enertech. I have no objection to government laboratories, but until we redress the balance and get more funding for R and D by private sector corporations, why are we building more government Crown corporations to whittle and diddle and fiddle away with the taxpayers' money?
Before closing, I would just like to ask why we cannot afford R and D in this country? I believe it is a matter which involves waste by this government. I have two examples. The other day one of my constituents received a padded bag containing a whole lot of bumper stickers and buttons, bilingual, printed both sides, imploring him to come and get more of these free goodies to put up in his plant and on the bumper of his automobile. They would be free. He could get as many as he wanted-to promote metric conversion! I wish to read the note which came back with this envelope, written by my constituent. He said:
As a taxpayer in this country I find this disgusting and immoral, the way you so freely spend our tax dollars on such garbage.
That is why we cannot afford to pay for science and technology. Metric advertising, bilingual games, wasteful double printing of government documents in both official languages, funny flags and all kinds of gismos are being purchased when we should be using that money to support scientific initiatives and to put our country back on the right track.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gerald Laniel (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE IN INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although the Minister of State for Science and Technology and Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) has indeed replied to the criticisms of the New Democratic Party and of the official opposition on this resolution, the motion contains statements which, I believe, lead nowhere. I know the hon. Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) would have

October 31, 1980
Science and Technology
wanted to be in the House himself this afternoon to refute again and doubly so these statements made by opposition members.
I want to remind the House that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce is presently in Paris where he is heading a delegation on trade co-operation between France and Canada and discussing such important issues as energy, raw materials, the automotive industry, aeronautics, telecommunications and other high technology industries. I will nonetheless do my best, Mr. Speaker, to show the House that the government's action in the areas of research and development and industrial strategy has been effective.

The government's record speaks for itself in harnessing the energy and talents of Canada's scientific community. We are indeed fortunate in possessing human resources in this country which are capable of undertaking research and development activities for the benefit of Canadian industry. However, when talking about research and development and its important role in the industrial development of the country, it is important to realize that research and development by themselves are not sufficient to create high technology companies which can face the competition which prevails in the international marketplace. It is important to view these issues in the full context of industrial innovation, including marketing and financing, which leads to the successful commercial exploitation of technology.
In many cases, Mr. Speaker, technological initiatives are bound to fail, not because of the technology itself or for lack of it, but rather because its marketing and financing aspects have been overlooked. Consequently, government programs and incentives must take into account the real possibilities of the market while encouraging technological development in Canada.

The federal government in general and the department which I represent, have long recognized this and over the past 20 years have introduced a range of incentive programs to encourage and support industrial innovation. 1 think it is fair to say that these programs are equal to, and probably better than and more generous than, those in many other developed countries. I wish to put before the House a few examples of programs that have benefited Canadian industry, most of which have been backed up at least at some time by government funding.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, the facts are eloquent, they speak for themselves. What we have heard to date, and what we still hear often from the New Democratic Party in this House and across the country, is what we call "parlage" in Quebec, or "just talk". The hon. member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong) spoke of the "failure of the government". He also spoke of "lip
service", of a policy of pious wishes, of a "do-nothing government", of the government inertia. But, what do they do? All in all, not much to convince the Quebec electorate that their proposals, which are supposed to be serious, can fit into the context of a stable and solid development of the Canadian economy.

I should like to give a few examples of the results of good government policies. 1 am speaking first of AES Data- [Translation]
-a Montreal company launched five years ago whose sales now reach $140 million. The CDC is its major shareholder and it spends over 8 percent of its sales revenue for research and development. I attended in person the inauguration of a new plant of the company Neeco Circuits System Ltd. of Montreal, last May, a company which now holds, or is starting to hold, an important rank in the field of electronic and printed circuits in Canada.

I want to speak also of other companies. MICOM, recently purchased by Phillips of the Netherlands, has had similar results in microelectronics, a critical area of expertise where Canada's capabilities are small but growing. Mitel, a company in this region, is undertaking a multi-year investment program which will raise its annual sales from under $10 million at the present time to some $90 million by 1984. Northern Telecom Limited, another example, is expected to bring its annual Ottawa production to $20 million in custom integrated circuits.
In the transportation sector the results are even more impressive. Government support for de Havilland, for example, has given this country an outstanding lead in the STOL technology.

The Pratt & Whitney Company of Longueil is the world leader as a manufacturer of small gas turbine engines for small aircrafts. The Bombardier Company is presently making expertise in the area of urban and semi-urban transportation. They manufacture trains for subways, LRC trains for export and it is developing new technologies in the area of railway transportation. They are also talking about manufacturing tramways for some Canadian and North American cities again.
And what about the great results of Canadair and Petro-Canada, Mr. Speaker?

Canada is a world leader in heavy water nuclear reactors, Mr. Speaker, and in the production of radioactive isotopes and devices for use in medical and industrial application.
Dome Petroleum has developed the capability to carry out exploration in ice-infested waters and Panarctic to drill in ice islands in the far north. Development of recovery and refining of heavy oils is another area of Canadian expertise.
October 31, 1980

That expertise did not come alone, Mr. Speaker. It is the result of a mixture of Canadian support with private enterprise. Many of these Canadian companies are part of a welcome phenomena involving the start up and growth of a variety of high technology concerns which has already transformed the Ottawa area into a kind of "silicon valley" of the north. The companies range from the biggest private laboratory in Canada, Bell-Northern Research Ltd. with 2,500 employees to Dipix Systems Limited which is involved in satellite data systems and has sales of about $1 million.
Ottawa's many high technology companies already employ 15,000 people, have a payroll of $200 million and estimated revenues of $500 million. If the present growth rate continues, by the end of this decade there will be more people employed by these industries in the Ottawa-Hull area than by the federal government.
The bulk of these skills was created in the fifties and sixties with the setting up of a number of high technology companies to serve government defence markets. Much of the original research in these areas was transferred from government labs. The increased emphasis in the sixties and seventies to contract out government research and development to industry, later supplemented by the location of Bell-Northern Research Ltd. and other companies in Ottawa, has allowed a critical mass of technical, scientific, entrepreneurial and managerial skills to develop which has been able to take advantage of the opportunities in the new technology fields. This, in turn, has attracted investor interest and what appears to be growing supply of venture capital to finance existing and new companies in the Ottawa area.
We often speak of government money, government grants or government monetary policy, Mr. Speaker. Last week I was present at the official opening of the second research centre of Xerox in Mississauga where I was told that the establishment of that multimillion-dollar centre was due to the convincing actions of the Hon. Alastair Gillespie, a former Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, coupled with the good monetary policy of the government. That centre will serve Xerox all over the world and will undertake research which has previously been spread over other locations.
The federal government contributed some $221 million in grants and contracts to industry in 1979-80 for industrially initiated research and development and that figure is expected to increase to $243 million in 1980-81. In terms of specific programs, such as the Enterprise Development Program of the department, some 225 product development projects were supported in 1979-80 for a total commitment of government funds of $58.1 million. From this commitment we estimate product sales of 2.55 billion will result over a period of five years.
In addition to providing assistance to Canadian companies, the federal government, through the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, of which I am parliamentary secretary to the minister, has a program to utilize more fully the
Science and Technology
scientific and technological capabilities in universities and to strengthen the technological infrastructure in Canada through the establishment of industrial research institutes, centres of advanced technologies and industrial research associations. Parenthetically I might mention that next week I will represent the minister at the official opening of the Canadian Welding Institute in Toronto where advanced technology is carried out. This technology is in the field of weldings, and it is done with the help of private enterprise-Alberta private enterprise and also, I believe the Alberta government and the Canadian government. The institute has the support of the well-qualified people we can find in this country.
This program has been highly successful in establishing Financially self-supporting organizations which contribute significantly to industrial development by providing expert research and development, testing and technical training services to industry on a contract basis. These services are especially useful to small and medium-sized companies. Of the 25 organizations established under this program, 15 are now financially self-sustaining and are no longer receiving government grants. One of these organizations is the one whose opening I will attend next Tuesday, The Canadian Welding Institute.
The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce has also financed the start-up of two industrial innovation centres. These centres are associated with universities with the objective of stimulating an increase in technological innovation and assisting private inventors and small and medium-sized technology-based companies to develop and commercialize inventions and technical ideas. Hon. members would be surprised how many people come to my office from different organizations who benefit from government programs or policies and who are very grateful for what we provide as a possible potential for development for the future not only for their associations but also for the industries they represent. [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of State for Science and Technology and Minister of the Environment has clearly shown the determination of the federal government in the field of research and development. He reiterated the commitment to raise to 1.5 per cent of the gross national product Canada's contribution to research and development. Of course it is not the federal government contribution alone, it is combined with the private sector's contribution. Research and development lead nowhere unless they are carried out with the involvement of private industry. The budget provides for increases in the economic development envelope and the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Weatherhead) will dwell on that in a few minutes.
Mr. Speaker, I think we can be proud of past accomplishments. There is still a long way to go. Industrial innovation will continue to be one of the key elements in developing and drafting future economic policies, although the details of these new policies are still in the preparatory stages, an aspect on

October 31, 1980
Science and Technology
new policies are still in the preparatory stages, an aspect on which the minister insisted here in the House recently when answering questions.
Funds have been earmarked for that purpose and it can be stated that these programs and these measures will be used at the right place, on the technological capacity of Canadian enterprise, on the availability of risk capital, particularly for small businesses, and finally on incentives to foreign subsidiaries to assume more autonomy and responsibility in developing operations on world markets for their new products.

This will involve an increased level of financial support for industry, including the possibility of increased support for major research and development projects. The emphasis will be on closer co-ordination with industry in order that Canadian companies can fully participate in the growing demand for the technological products of the 1980s.
It is clear that the federal government recognizes the need for Canadian industry to increase substantially its efforts in the development and commercial application of new Canadian technology. Industrial innovation will have an increasingly important impact on many of the critical decisions companies will be required to make not only regarding the design of products and services or the choice of equipment and processes but also in the planning of future operating facilities, distribution activities and information systems. The impact of new technology in Canada is of fundamental importance to the future of virtually every company, and those companies which are not dynamic will not be successful. This will be taken fully into account in the strategic planning process of this government, which has put forward not only in its budget but also in its energy policy programs which look to the future and not to the past as we have heard in much of the criticism this afternoon.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE IN INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad this afternoon to have the opportunity to join in this debate on the motion presented by the New Democratic Party, which reads as follows:
That this House condemns the government for having failed to harness the energies and talents of Canada's scientific and technological community in the development of an industrial strategy which would draw on Canada's traditional resource base, on our manufacturing strength, and on our new high technology industries.
I was surprised and delighted to see that motion. I was surprised that the New Democratic Party would condemn the government, and I was delighted that its members would choose this very appropriate way to call attention to their dislike of the way the government is behaving.
I strongly support this motion. Examples of the ways in which technologies have been advanced by governments have been brought forward very well by other members this afternoon. Examples of technologies which have helped this country are Mitel, Spar Aerospace, heavy water plants and nuclear power facilities.
All these are areas in which the government has helped and in which through science and technology we have helped to advance our country and our industrial base. The problem is that too little has been done and without any sustained, programmed, controlled and organized approach.
1 would like to address this problem in a very specific way this afternoon by referring to the area of energy research and development. In this way I can give the best single example of the difficulties we experience in our research and development programs in Canada. I think this is the best single example to illustrate the absence of technical understanding on the part of the government, the best single example to show the squandering of our natural resources and the best single example to show the wasting of our human potential.
Our energy resource base has proved a magnificent endowment. We have tremendous potentials not only in renewable energy resources like hydroelectric power, and fossil fuels, but also in biomass that is renewable. We have uranium deposits which give us an almost inexhaustible resource, if we choose to tap it.
Even at this time we are a net exporter of energy. All the time we have been addressing our energy resources, and we have proved that we can consume, but to this point we have not shown that we can effectively reduce the consumption for which we are responsible.
Back in the 1960s about the time of the Sputnik there was a tremendous resurgence of interest in the technological field, and at that time the economy was very healthy. There was a glow about the technological community which was expressed by people cultivating scientific interests, going to university and taking scientific courses with the result that we were developing a research base in this country. It was a weak base, but it was developing at that time.
But then something happened. Back in about 1967 or 1968 things started to change and the resource and research base, which had been developing, started to diminish and dwindle. We started to experience increased costs for social programs and development of that type. Our economy, which was outwardly-healthy in the 1960s, started to fail and people stopped going to universities and entering into scientific programs which would give them the ability to undertake scientific endeavours in the country. At the same time, the Medical Council of Canada, the Canada Council and the National Research Council decreased their level of funding to universities.
One of the other consistent problems we have had in Canada, in addition to the lack of opportunities we have with our human resource base and our energy resource base, is a very low capital situation. Not much capital is available for investment. This has been a consistent problem through the 1960s, 1970s and on into the 1980s. This is something with which we have to live. We do not have the capital we need to invest in large energy developments and in our energy resources.
October 31, 1980

1 would like to quote a passage which I think is relevant. It goes like this:
"Would you tell me please which way 1 ought to go from here?" asked Alice. "That depends a good deal on where you want to get to" said the cat.
Some of my hon. friends may recognize that. Alice, 1 think, was addressing a problem which governments have to address.
I have no way of telling where this government wanted to get to, but there is no question about the course of action that was followed. It is expressed simply by the percentage of the gross national product devoted to energy research and development. In 1967, it was 1.4 per cent; in 1980, it was 0.9 per cent of the gross national product. We have been maintaining an unearned lifestyle on the base of the natural resources of our country.
Back in the early 1970s, the National Energy Board predicted that this country had an oil surplus. We found out, to our regret, back in about 1973, that that was not the case. Then came the oil imports. Instead of responding to the technological challenges, our philosophical wizard leaders either through neglect or ignorance, continued to shelter us from the realities of rising energy costs and, at the same unfortunate moment, kept our alternate energy resources and conservation technology from competing. The burst of federal research and development effort and scientific achievement which led to Candu and oil sands extraction was short-lived and it has been a long, dry decade since any major energy technological achievement.
In 1967, the Science Council recognized the importance of technological sovereignty and also, called for the development of sound programs for the use of conservation and the replenishing of resources. I would just like to quote briefly from its annual report:
We in Canada must extend, and, even more important, apply our advantages and overcome our special difficulties or even turn them into assets. Our resources of money and manpower are limited; therefore we must apportion them wisely, concentrating them in areas that are important to the nation, socially, economically and scientifically.
The folly of not appreciating the importance of these concepts demonstrates vividly the technological gap that has existed in the heads of successive governments. Where we stand today with energy developments is vivid evidence of the flaws in our political leadership.
Today, in energy research and development, conventional fuels research and development is done largely by provincial governments, with only $10 million in 1980 contributed by the federal government. The recent renewable energy agreements with the provinces seemed to be of some help, but they were late, and even with these we can expect to achieve only about 5 per cent of our energy resources in the renewable area, excluding hydro by the 2,000. So in spite of this immense potential, we are not developing our energy resources. In fact, we now have shortfalls in energy supply that would indicate rationing.
PERD is the panel for energy research and development which co-ordinates all the energy research and development in the country under EMR. There are five separate areas. I will not go through them now, Mr. Speaker, because of lack of
Science and Technology
time, but they include conservation, fossil fuel, nuclear energy, renewable energy, energy transmission, and transportation. They each have their own budgets. In six years they have spent a total of $760 million. That is their total investment, even though back in 1974 we had a pretty good idea of what was happening, both in terms of our oil supplies, the OPEC countries, and the oil embargo situation.
The long-term energy supply potential of this and every other nation rests either in solar, nuclear fission, or nuclear fusion. Only in one area, in the area of nuclear fission, have we in any way been able to achieve what we should have achieved in the area of research and development to help our energy supply situation. The National Research Council, with a total budget in six years of $44 million, has been expected to do the research and development in hydraulics, solar, biomass and wind. The National Research Council has a very special problem. It is a problem of management, and this is not a unique problem in terms of scientific communities in Canada. As a Crown corporation, NRC has been expected both to manage and to do the research with the funds it has available. At one and the same time, the scientists are expected to be managers. We have to appreciate now that this is a very important aspect of the difficulties we are having with research and development in this country because what has happened is that people who are normal scientific people have been thrown into a milieu where they are required both to manage the resources and do the research. There are very few people who have this double capacity.
One of the other problems which the NRC is facing is a lack of enthusiasm. This lack of enthusiasm stems from a number of causes. Funding is one part of it because it has been inconsistent; it has been up and down, programs have been switched and people have lost heart because of the difficulties in maintaining an effective program. People are unenthusiastic because there has been no understanding, at the level of government, of their problems and of the importance of the work they are doing. Finally, they are losing enthusiasm because even when the funding is available, because of regulatory restraints they are not able to engage people to take advantage of the funding. They cannot hire people when necessary even though the funding is there.
The final point, which has to do with political control, presents the National Research Council with a particular problem because of the technological gap which exists between their level of activity and people in the government, people at the ministerial level and at all government levels. This gap is widening today. The minister and the people in charge do not understand the technological achievements and therefore cannot keep up in terms of dealing effectively with management problems. So we end up with a situation where the technocrats are in control of science and there is very little relationship between scientists and the government.
Fusion is an example 1 am going to use in terms of the difficulties of NRC because it is a subject on which the minister made a statement. I should like to quote his comment

October 31, 1980
Science and Technology
before the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates of July 8 of this year. He said at that time, talking about fusion: When I say skeptical, I mean that literally-it does not mean I have taken a decision one way or the other. I think the case still has to be made that Canada should be involved in fusion research in a major way.
The history of fusion research in Canada is very interesting, but in the short time available to me I would just like to say that we have at least three separate areas in Canada which are competent in fusion research. We have people such as Dr. Skarsgard at the university of Saskatchewan who is respected in the international community as a very prominent fusion researcher. We have people in Canada in different provinces who have been very interested in trying to bring the INTOR project to this country; that project, I understand, may well be cancelled because of the situation in Afghanistan and the international climate. But that situation need not prevail indefinitely. It is a situation which may not, in fact, stop INTOR. We can still be involved in an international program if we have the desire. Hydro Quebec is another good example. They have a fusion project and a research reactor which they would like to develop and use. They are very concerned now, because of federal attitude, that they will no longer be able to do this.
In 1979 the National Research Council dedicated $3.1 million to fusion research. In 1980 the commitment was only $2.9 million. The International Energy Agency commented on this. It was concerned about the low level of funding to fusion research in Canada. We are concerned about fusion research because we will not be able to keep up with the international community. We will not be able to keep our hand in at the table when we are talking about technological advances which can help the country.
I should like to try to explain the importance of this. Look at some of the advantages of the fusion research program. Quite short of actually producing the electrical power of fusion, we have the advantage of development technology in a number of ways. Indeed it is a potential energy source, both at home and abroad. It is a potential complement to the Candu system- and this is something which is poorly understood-because it can help develop fuels for the Candu system. It can help with other technologies from electronics to the programs trying to achieve direct electrical energy conversion. It can help in developing special materials for use in reactors. Finally, it can help in the area of international co-operation.
I should like to refer to the Science Council of Canada Report of June 1979 which reads as follows:
International co-operation is essential to ensure that Canada remains at the leading edge of scientific and technological research, to avoid unnecessary duplication of work done by others, and to develop the capacity to adopt and adapt foreign technology to its own advantage. In selected instances, especially when dealing with complex technologies, Canada need not "go it alone" because of concern that co-operation would result in a secondary role. On the contrary, Canadians should systematically assure equity in international developments through practical and responsible sharing, and through comparative strenghts based on unique high leverage opportunities.
For whatever reasons, the Minister of State of Science and Technology (Mr. Roberts) does not understand.
The United States has a permanent science and technology committee with a number of subcommittees. It has a support staff of 80 permanent people for the committee and subcommittees. It dedicates 2.5 per cent of its gross national product to science and technology. It is surpassing us in all energy technologies with the exception of the Candu fission reactor and tar sands and heavy oil developments. It uses private enterprise management systems to manage the research and development effectively.
The government must identify the importance of science and technology to the country. As each year passes, we see there is an increase in societal dependence on technology, an increasing dependence on foreign technology with a branch plant mentality for technology being adopted and imports of technology into this country instead of developing them here. Each year there is an increasing gap between politicians and technology. In the end we are leaving our destinities in the hands of technocrats.
As each year passes, shrinking geographical boundaries and population expansion come close to the limits. If needs in energy and other resources are not met in the global sense, we run an increasing risk of global conflict. We can help meet many of these needs as well as provide important improvements in our own country. We can provide improvements in employment, in our balance of trade payments, environmental control and national self-sufficiency in energy.
I personally believe we can start this procedure by establishing an effective energy R and D program and an effective over-all R and D program. This effort would be significantly assisted by several measures. First, by providing independent private enterprise management systems for bodies such as the National Research Council. Second, by relieving R and D functions from any restrictive regulatory controls on personnel. Third, by aiming for continued research and development funding of at least 2.5 per cent or more of the gross national product. Fourth, by developing interacting effective liaison for business, university and government. Fifth, by expanding and maintaining international involvement and co-operation where appropriate. Sixth, by establishing tax and government financial assistance and procurement practices to assist private enterprise research and development and to provide markets for the purchase of first products. Seventh, by re-establishing the credibility of the scientific university community through financial support, project grants and constant co-operation.
