Eighth, by the establishment of a parliamentary standing committee on R and D. Ninth, by providing political leadership which is sensitive, informed and committed. Tenth, by providing a permanent full-time R and D minister.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE IN INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate today. I listened with some interest to members on the government side and I must say I have not been convinced of one single matter relating to either the budget or their position in relation to science and technology. This afternoon I intend to support, particularly in relation to the inherent problems of the forest sector, some of the state-
October 31, 1980

ments made by members opposite and explain why our motion is inherently correct.
Canada's scientific and technological sector is Canada's first industry. The forest industry is now in a rapid decline. The universities of this country are not producing anywhere near the number or level of experts required in the forest industry, and the low level of funds delivered by the federal and provincial governments is the reason.
This week's budget did not contain one word about Canada's largest single economic sector. By not placing a single word in the budget about the forest sector, it totally justifies the motion put forward by the hon. member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong). In my view the government condemned itself on Tuesday.
I should like to outline exactly what is happening in the forest sector before getting into some of my specific recommendations relating to R and D. Not many Canadians are aware that only 35 per cent of Canada is treed and that only a fraction of that area is still harvestable first growth. Forest products in Canada are the largest single net source of revenue, particularly to the federal government, with approximately $20 billion in exports this year. I must point out that it provides a livelihood for slightly over 10 per cent of the labour force in Canada and employs in excess of 1.3 million Canadian men and women.
Both the yield and supply of forest products are dwindling. For example, British Columbia produces about 80 per cent of the softwood lumber for Canada, 50 per cent of the pulp, and 30 per cent of the softwood lumber for United States market. Supplies are declining particularly in the province of British Columbia which is the largest single geographic region producing forest products. There will be shortages in every region of British Columbia within 5 to 20 years. Most of the largest, most productive areas will face shortages by the middle of this decade. By the turn of the century another 25 per cent of the forest land will have been shaved away for such uses as agriculture, urban and rural sprawl, rights of way and parks. Most of that land will be prime valley bottom, the most important and productive area for the growth of forests.
The public are the true stewards of forest lands, yet neither Ottawa nor any of the provinces have really accepted that challenge and set up public advisory committees to deal with the very serious question of what uses forest lands should be put to. Rather than accepting that challenge at the government level and allowing the public to become involved, they are allowing an increasing number of conflicts to arise. Rather than achieving some kind of resolution of these problems in advance, we will see conflicts between fishermen and loggers, between miners and foresters. Inaction will create serious social problems which really do not need to occur.
One serious question we have to face-and certainly the government has never faced it-is how to maintain volume without entering further into the regime of bad forest practices in which we are presently involved. The budget gouges western and northern Canada to the benefit of Liberal patronage programs in the United States. I do not make either of those
Science and Technology
statements lightly. The funds for research and development in the following areas are examples of where I feel a considerable number of dollars should have been placed. I am speaking of hundreds of millions of dollars. I think, for example, of the harvesting and utilization of trees down to the size of ten centimetres. Right now in Canada there simply is not the development, either at the university level or within the industry, for the types of technology required for harvesting and utilization. On the northern Pacific coast one of our most serious problems is the leaving of small trees in the bush under nine inches in diameter at the butt. A lot of the timber slightly larger than that, particularly hemlock and species such as that, are simply dumped into the ocean after being brought out because the industry finds it cheaper to allow those trees to go to waste. So they drift up on the beach where they have a very serious and damaging impact. This is another area where the federal government has clear jurisdiction and should be involved. As these trees wash in and out with the tide they break off the kelp, disturb intertidal life, break the barnacles and that type of life off the rocks, and cause a serious decline of the inner beach areas. This has an impact on fisheries on the Pacific coast and a general impact on our whole biological system in British Columbia. I would say a similar situation exists in the maritimes as well.
It is in these areas that research and development and forward-looking policies would benefit us all rather than allowing these problems to accumulate until very serious damage has been done. A government which had any sort of progressive or imaginative policies would be dealing with these things now.
A crucial problem which we have experienced this year, perhaps more than in most years, has been the serious forest fire problem. An area about six times larger than the area which will be cut this year was burned, particularly in Ontario and Manitoba. The government is doing nothing in terms of research and development to utilize and harvest those burned trees so that they can be put to a wide variety of uses, as has been demonstrated in other areas of the world. The national allowable cut in Canada is now 200 million cubic metres per year with about 150 million cubic metres per year actually being harvested.
The area that was burned this year was larger in size than Great Britain. It consisted of some 240,000 square kilometres. Interestingly enough, that is almost exactly the same size as the area which has been left. It is an area which was cut in the past several decades; it was formerly productive land and now it lies unsatisfactorily restocked. I think we should take a close look at that. The industry harvested generally the valley bottoms and heavy rainfall areas that had been cut. There are washouts, the soil disappears and the companies are not forced to go back in to do proper reforestation and silviculture. Those areas lie idle. History speaks for itself in relation to issues such as this. We can see enormous, barren areas, for example, in northern Africa and other parts of the world which were

Science and Technology
improperly harvested and never restocked and have turned into desert.
Where is the federal government? Where are the funds for R and D, for such things as hog fuel, briquettes and development for industrial use? Certainly the forests will become one of our major areas of energy production and we simply are not moving into that area at all.
Cutting, milling trades and training in the use of hardwoods are classic examples of small, almost cottage-sized industries which could be utilized in the maritimes, throughout Quebec, Ontario and very much so in western Canada for such products as furniture, wall and floor coverings. The reason you do not see a lot of cottage or small hand-logging operations in these areas is that the R and D has not been done and is not being done for that type of utilization, for providing practical small kiln operations, small milling operations for the individual tradesman and producer. Twenty per cent of the merchan-disable volume of timber in Canada right now is hardwood. Yet it is only 5 per cent of the harvest. That is a shameful thing for a country to be admitting when such woods as we see here in the House of Commons may never be seen again in this country if we do not get some decent silvicultural practices under way. Basic efficiency is what research and development should encourage.
In relation to milling, for example, some of the small countries which have no indigenous forest population are the ones which are moving the most quickly. In the area of laser and sonar the Japanese have moved very quickly. Last year, 30 per cent of the cypress or yellow cedar which was moved from British Columbia and sent directly to Japan was milled in Japan. There they make full use of laser and sonar production whereby the log is actually sized by sonar; they know where the knots, tapers and cracks are and they know where the bark is. It is completely sized, it is computerized and it is cut with almost no sawdust and almost no waste.
For a country like Canada to be simply mining our forests at a time when that kind of technology is being created is just not good enough. If we simply had the R and D to bring some of that fundamental technology here so we could expand it and make full use of the products we have here in Canada, making not only more jobs in R and D but more jobs within the industry, it would avoid the conflicts we are likely to see in terms of multiple resource use. The complexity of the situation is compounded by a government that simply will not act in an imaginative fashion and get the R and D money moving.
The great grab of prime first-growth in Canada is almost over, yet the forest sector still accounts for over 18 per cent of our exports. I am sure there are not many members sitting in the House today who recognize that it makes a larger contribution to the Canadian economy than agriculture, mining, fishing and petroleum put together.
Federal funds available last year were less than $130 million. I differ from my friends to the right here who say they made a dramatic expansion in last year's budget. They did make a number of progressive moves, certainly in relation to putting in place an assistant deputy minister to deal with
forestry at the national level. I certainly compliment them for that move, and not the members on the opposite side.
Less than $200 million will be spent this year on R and D in the forest industry. I would point out that this amount is exactly half of what was put aside for R and D in relation to forestry ten years ago. A decade ago we were putting in twice as much in terms of real dollars. I think that is a pretty shameful comment on the minister who rose in the House earlier today and indicated that he really was going to move hard in the field of research and development. Out of the $20 billion in relation to the export of products in the forest industry, only $35 million, as was pointed out earlier today, will be spent on research and development in this industry. This is less than two-tenths of one per cent of the economic value and is a shameful comment in relation to this industry, not only in Canada but anywhere in the world.
There is nothing in the budget, even with a national economic and unemployment disaster on our horizon. It is quite clear that the shaving away of forest land and the serious problems which are occurring now are caused by prime cuts which have come off and are being replaced by much smaller second growth. Quite frequently, for example, when red cedar or Sitka spruce or Douglas firs are cut down, the second growth you naturally get back is composed of alder or some of the less valuable species such as hemlock. This certainly happens in the province of British Columbia for which I can speak, knowing the forest industry in that region quite well. Yet such simple techniques as better reforestation-and when I say that I mean the entirety of silviculture from the collection of the seeds, to the growing of the small seedling, to planting it and caring for it, in terms of thinning processes and so on-is good investment. As my hon. friend from Regina East pointed out, investments of that sort are good investments. You invest a few pennies today and you collect many dollars down the line. It is only a very shortsighted government, interested in clutching and grabbing straws close at hand, which would overlook the importance of reforestation in Canada today. To invest a few million dollars in the next few years would create billions of dollars over the next 20 years. Forest management on the east slope of the Rockies in Alberta would do a number of very profound things, not only in relation to wildlife, the aesthetics of the area and the potential forest harvesting; it would allow more water to drain into the river systems, which provide Canada with its very strong and important agricultural base. But nothing is being done either in the budget or in policies of the government to deal with this very serious and pressing problem. Better processing would save a minimum of 20 per cent of the product yield.
Earlier I mentioned laser and sonar technology. It is an area in which Canada, of all the countries in the world, should be moving ahead the fastest, but we are not. At least 1.5 per cent of the forest industry gross product should be allocated to research and development. As I said earlier, the figure is presently only .2 per cent. We must move ahead by at least a multiple of 7 per cent or 8 per cent before we will even be on a
October 31, 1980

standing with some of the very small countries which have no indigenous forest populations.
Increased expenditures on research and development will not only give us a better, more saleable, less expensive product, but will give us faster growing trees and more jobs. Again, it comes back to the energy sector. 1 recognize that the Canadian Forest Service and Federal Research Service are doing something in the area of small, rapid growth tree harvesting in their investigations of methanol production for possible replacement. 1 think it is an excellent idea. One of these days members of this House will wake up and realize that gas and petroleum were produced tens of thousands of years ago from growing plants. Ultimately, the light will go on in our minds and we will recognize that we will be required to obtain our energy from the sun, through plants and biomass. Research and development is an investment that would pay off handsomely. Instead, what we have is a Liberal policy, that, rather than pay-off, gives us lay-off, in excess of 1,000 people a day.
The staff decrease in the forest service is 138 this year at a time when we are not even approaching sustained yield. The forests of this nation are being mined, particularly by federal forest policy. Less than five cents of each dollar of tax revenue going to the federal-provincial coffers is being spent on silviculture. The Canadian Forestry Association, for example, estimates that 20 per cent of the land is receiving little or inadequate regeneration at the present time, and that is a 1980 figure.
That figure is quite different from the figure given by the minister earlier today. He said that 12 per cent of our prime forest land is inadequately stocked. We can quibble over the difference between the word "little" and the word "inadequate", but certainly he estimates about half of what is estimated by the Canadian Forestry Association. However, he does admit that we are falling back in restocking our forest lands by at least 500,000 acres a year. I took these figures from a recent speech made by the minister. Yet he wants to increase the cut by 50 per cent by the year 2000. In my opinion that is total, irresponsible Liberal hypocrisy. When one sees the figures on what is happening in the forest sector, to propose to increase the cut by 50 per cent without investing any R and D money is absolutely hypocritical. The Minister of State for Science and Technology and Minister of the Environment once said:
Knowledgeable opinion is unanimous that Canadians must spend more money to maintain our country's forests.
Then he went on to say that Canadian forest service has 50 per cent fewer staff than in 1968 when the Prime Minister came to office, and that the purchasing value of the budget this year is less than half of what it was nine years ago. It is a very shameful comment on R and D in the forest service in this country. The minister also said:
It is my intention to strengthen federal involvement in forestry.
That is an absolutely ludicrous statement. How can he strengthen investment by cutting research and development, cutting staff and cutting the budget in half? It is the ultimate in double talk and attempted public deception. It is time we
Science and Technology
matched the annual cut with annual production on those lands which have been and are being cut. Is that not sustained yield? For example, 13 per cent of our pulp now goes to newsprint and 30 per cent to wrapping paper. Where is the research and development in this country on recycling that paper or the government input to see that recycling becomes a real part of conservation in Canada? Think of the impact on jobs and conservation if the money used for the goose and beaver ads were used for conservation purposes instead of for sheer political propaganda.
This brings me to my concluding remarks concerning what I call the fall-down effect. First, the forest base is shrinking, as is demonstrated by scientific evidence. Second, second growth which is smaller in diameter and smaller in volume of wood will create an impact on the industry. Third, there are fewer R and D dollars coming from the federal government. Fourth, there are fewer innovations in silviculture, pest control and enhanced growth. Fifth, there are fewer new products for local and international markets-this, again, will have an impact on our balance of payments and industry within Canada. Sixth, there is less education for conservation and product recycling, and this comes at the same time as the government is cutting back funds to post-secondary education in the R and D field of forestry.
There are fewer scientists being produced due to the lack of these funds and there are fewer staff due to the Liberal cutbacks which I have already outlined and can be confirmed in this year's main estimates. There are lost jobs due to the economics of scale in the industry, and this, too, is creating a very serious problem. None of my information has been disputed in this House, nor do I expect that it will be in the near future unless the government completely changes its policies.
The Liberals are eager to get into the profits of gas and oil in western Canada. In my view there lies the true nature of that party. In relation to the forest industry and to R and D, it has put nothing into these areas even when they are on the decline. But because prices are beginning to move up in the oil and gas industry, the Liberal hand goes in to grab.
Today's message is not new. In 1871 Sir John A. Macdonald said:
We are recklessly destroying the timber of Canada and there is scarcely the possibility of replacing it.
That was said well over 100 years ago. I will conclude with two very short statements. In one area of my riding a Crown corporation ordered five million seedlings from Victoria this year, but only one million will be delivered and by no means will all those seedlings survive. A totally new, totally Canadian-owned operation to make pressboard in Smithers, in my riding, was turned down by this government through DREE in favour of a foreign-owned eastern Canadian operation. Those two statements speak for themselves, as does today's motion, and it is all because of the budget introduced on Tuesday.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE IN INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend, the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Roberts), described earlier this afternoon the

Science and Technology
action of the government in spurring greater research and development in Canadian industry. Innovation and technical change are central to Canada's future manufacturing performance. They have and will continue to receive very strong government support. In addition there were excellent examples of practical results of the government's recent programs outlined earlier today by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) and the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Laniel).
But greater effort in R and D and innovation, however critical to our industrial strength, is by itself, not a sufficient response to the competitive pressures that Canada faces in the 1980s and beyond. Drastically higher prices for energy and changes in the international trading environment are only two of the most obvious of these pressures. Exposure to ever more aggressive competition and import penetration from the newly industrialized countries, in standard technology products, and from a number of developing countries in low technology, labour-intensive products and resource commodities are also extremely significant factors in the new economic environment that confronts the traditional industrialized world.
A successful response to this environment will call for imaginative government action and leadership on a broad front. Without such a government commitment, there is no assurance that Canadian economic performance will be maximized or that we can even keep pace. I want to take a few moments to sketch out the dimensions of this commitment.
An overriding government task is to seek to maximize efficient activity in all regions of Canada based on economic strengths and, especially, the resource strengths that can spearhead development in the west and Atlantic regions, although with benefits accruing to all of Canada. To achieve this, the government has recognized a need for developmental assistance to ensure that major growth opportunities, for instance, in advanced technology industries and in resource supply and further processing sectors, are captured, and measures to ensure that Canadian firms are able to participate competitively in supplying the engineering expertise, the equipment and the new technology required for the expected massive energy and resource development in the coming years.
These are necessary because it is far from assured that the development of our energy supplies will bring significant longterm industrial benefits.
Another overriding consideration, closely related to the constitutional reform process, concerns the strengthening and maintenance of the Canadian common market. In a world characterized by economic entities five to ten times more populated than our own, such as the United States, Japan and the European economic community, the last thing Canada needs is fragmentation of its own domestic market. On the contrary, we need to find the means for establishing and maintaining the largest possible domestic market as an essential prerequisite of a more efficient, more productive and more internationally competitive economy. This is one of the fundamental objectives of constitutional reform, yet it is an objective on which we have just begun to make progress.
The government is also committed to, first, adjustment policies focussing on productive investment rather than subsidy to encourage the movement of resources to strong and potentially strong industries and potentially strong subsectors in less dynamic industries at a rate sensitive to social considerations.
Second, it is committed to influencing firms with a significant impact on the economy to pursue innovation and product development in Canada, expansion of exports and sourcing of equipment, components and services on a competitive basis from Canadian suppliers.
Third, this government is committed to encouraging Canadian ownership and control of this country's productive assets and ensuring that foreign investment, to the extent that we require it, adds to our ability to take full advantage of the opportunities that are opened up to us. Fourth, the government is committed to assistance to firms to obtain access to and develop markets abroad, including the development of a concept for a national trading corporation and of more effective export financing programs.
These measures in industrial development, all of which, by the way, are consistent with the government's campaign and throne speech commitments, are not an exhaustive accounting of the elements of a national industrial policy. Nevertheless, they demonstrate the wide range of needs and problems which the government is addressing, and addressing imaginatively, flexibly and co-operatively with business and labour to stimulate the maximum realization of the country's economic potential.
The federal budget of last Tuesday states that the total increase in the economic envelope expenditures over a three-year period, from 1980-1981 to 1983-1984 will amount to $6.49 billion. Of the $6.49 billion, approximately $4 billion will be spent on new western initiatives. Particular attention in the western initiatives program will be directed to infrastructure development, such as grain handling and transportation, which is intrinsic to economic development in the west and also to industrial diversification in the west.
Over the three years, in addition to the $4 billion on the western initiatives program, there will be at least $2.49 billion allocated to research and development, expansion and modernization of industrial capacity, and other elements of the government's economic development plans.
The budget also pays special attention to the economic development problems of less developed areas. The speech announced a special allocation of $350 million to deal with the industrial restructuring and labour adjustment problems in regions of particular need. There is also a new investment tax credit which will pay to investors 50 per cent of manufacturing investments made in high unemployment and low income regions of the country.
The energy package is particularly important to the promotion of economic development. The made-in-Canada pricing schedule will ensure maintenance of a strong competitive edge
October 31, 1980

for domestic manufacturers. The energy package also envisions the expenditure of enormous sums of money which will have multiplying economic development impacts. For example, the oil substitution component will comprise $1.6 billion of expenditures on things such as conversion grants and conversion of federal buildings, which imply great opportunities for industries suppling conversion equipment. Similarly, the $1.15 billion that will be spent on conservation and renewables will involve industrial development opportunities and government assistance to improve energy efficiency and so modernize and enhance productivity of a great number of industrial plants throughout the country.
Finally, the greater control the federal government is obtaining over the development of the energy sector through new regulations and the new regulations and the new treatment of Canada lands will ensure that Canadian industries in all parts of the country can share in the industrial benefits of energy development. For example, the new oil and gas act will ensure that a high level of Canadian goods and services is employed in oil and gas activities carried out on Canada lands. Applicants for exploration and production rights will have to demonstrate how their operations will bring industrial and employment benefits to Canada, both in the region of interest, and elsewhere in the country. Where applicable, companies will be expected to put in place special training and employment measures, particularly for native Canadians.
I want to stress that in the task of putting together the complex of policies and programs necessary to ensure a bright
Science and Technology
industrial future for Canada, the government has and will continue to rely on the advice and co-operation from the Canadian public, especially groups representing business and labour. Recent examples, such as the Tier I and Tier II committees and the Hatch committee, indicate that when business and government focus on specific problems or actions, wide areas of agreement can be found. Currently there is the important work of the Blair major projects task force which is examining the long-term contribution of major capital projects to the growth of the Canadian industrial and technological base. Mentioned as well should be the important but less visible contacts of ministers and government officials on an ongoing basis with government and labour.
We are now moving from agreement to action on many fronts. I expect that my colleague, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) will be in a position to announce some of these measures to the House in the near future. I am encouraged by the new interest expressed by the opposition parties in industrial policy and hope that when the government announces these measures it will have their full co-operation and support.
May I say again that I was pleased to take part in this debate. May we call it five o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
